speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these two questions asked by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) seek the disclosure of legal opinions received by the government. Upon making inquiries I am informed by my deputy, Mr. Varcoe, that this is the first time within his knowledge that production of opinions of this sort has ever been sought. I have also conferred with Mr. McGregor, commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act, with regard to these two questions, and, after that conference, I am of the view that the government should refuse to disclose any of the legal opinions in connection with any combines report.
It should be remembered that these opinions usually take the form of a review and analysis of the relevant parts of the report. Usually the opinions are quite long, and analyse the report from beginning to end. On occasions they refer to the transcript of

evidence upon which the report is based. Possible defences in fact or in law, and how they may be met by the crown, are usually commented upon and appraised. The result is a communication between lawyer and client which is and should be privileged from disclosure, because in most, if not in all cases, such disclosure would give the accused and their counsel a preview of the crown's case. This would have a most prejudicial effect upon the prosecution of the case. The government therefore takes the position that it cannot table opinions of this sort.
Under the circumstances I am prepared to drop the questions. However, I would ask the minister to let me confirm this.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, November 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 144, to amend the Combines Investigation Act-Mr. Garson-Mr. Dion in the Chair.
On section 1-Attorney General of Canada may institute and conduct prosecutions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so far as the strengthening of the Combines Investigation Act is concerned, we of the C.C.F. party are thoroughly in accord. As I said in the letter which I wrote to the present Prime Minister on December 4, 1947, we believe not only that the act needs strengthening but also that the combines investigation commissioner should have sufficient staff to deal with what we believe to be the large number of cases of price fixing and combinations we find in this country at the present time. Incidentally I might remark that the act does not deal with the question of monopolies as the anti-trust legislation of the United States, the Sherman Act, does.
We have long felt that if the government and the house believe in competition and free enterprise there should be legislation on the statute book to prevent private monopolies and combinations. I want to be specific; I do not believe the anti-trust legislation of the United States has been successful in meeting the needs of that country in relation to combines and monopolies. The only way to deal with a monopoly is to bring it under some sort of public control. As my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, said yesterday, when an industry reaches the stage where it can exploit a community, at least it should be brought under effective control, which I believe involves national ownership of that monopoly. On the other hand, the majority of the members elected to the house do not believe that; consequently either the act should be strengthened or another act should be placed on the statute book to deal specifically with the matter.
I want to make one or two brief comments about some of the points that have been made in connection with what the minister has said, and what I have said, in this debate.
The minister's defence of the non-observance of a vital clause of the act is based entirely on wartime experience and alleged wartime agreements. That is not the point. The point is that the activities about which complaint is made in the report stem from the years before the war. The practices about 45781-138
Combines Investigation Act which complaint is made were carried through the wartime period, and we believe into the period that followed the war. Consequently I do not think his contention if it were accepted is a valid one.
There is no documentary evidence to support the contention that immunities existed. There is nothing in the record except one interesting memorandum of June 21, 1943, indicating that a discussion occurred between the minister, the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, and certain officials, about the position of the subsidies, their implications, and so on. Let me refer to the paragraph reading in part as follows:
... it may be desirable or necessary to place a minimum price on sales of flour in order to prevent any miller from taking undue advantage of the arrangement to reduce domestic flour prices at the expense of the government.
There is nothing in the record indicating that this was actually brought to a final conclusion. Moreover, I say again, as I have said several times-and I think it has been overlooked-that if the milling industry had told the combines investigator, and had presented substantial evidence of it, either documentary or oral, to the commissioner, that an understanding had been reached during the war concerning these matters and concerning the immunity of the milling industry under the Combines Investigation Act, at that point all further investigation would have stopped, and a report would not have been made of the kind which was to be placed before the people of Canada by the combines investigator.
I have not seen Mr. McGregor since long before this controversy began, but I am satisfied, from what I know of his past work and his reputation in the civil service, that if that had been done, this report would not have been made. I want to be quite clear about that, because it is vital to the discussion.
There is one paragraph in the memorandum of June 21, 1943, which I still find puzzling, and as a matter of fact I think the minister did too. There are these words:
The foregoing is to be treated very confidentially and not made known to either the Administration, or to the industry at this time.
In this document, which the minister was good enough to send across to me- it is the one that was omitted from the return-"administration" has a capital "A". Mr. Donald Gordon was present at this conference, and he was the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board; consequently it cannot refer to the wartime prices and trade board. The only interpretation I have been able to place upon it is that "Administration" means that this tentative understanding,

Combines Investigation Act which was never brought to a final conclusion, should remain confidential and not be made known to the flour milling industry or the government. If that is so, surely it is exceedingly strange. If the treasury board and the government were to be protected as alleged, why on earth should such an understanding be withheld from the government of the day. Surely if this was in any measure -and I mean the suggestions made in the memorandum-an understanding with a view to protecting government expenditures, why should it be kept secret from the government of the day? I ask the minister to explain that, because if I am wrong I want to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I did explain it. Perhaps my hon. friend was not listening, and I certainly could not blame him for that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I was out of the chamber, attending a committee meeting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: When one speaks for two and a half hours he cannot expect to hold the attention of everyone for the whole time. I explained that in these terms: that I had asked that question myself, since the question suggested itself at once to anyone reading the memorandum. The explanation given to me is set out in Hansard. It is that they did not want the negotiations complicated by premature disclosures to the industry on the one hand or to the government on the other. They wanted no word of this discussion to go back prematurely at that stage through the people who had participated in it, to the government and to the industry, which seems to me a very natural desire. I hope my hon. friend realizes that the Minister of Finance himself was present at that meeting, so there was nothing sinister at all about this. I might also add that in substance the arrangement subsequently formalized by orders in council, notwithstanding what my hon. friend says, was the arrangement contemplated in that memorandum. The only difference I recall at the moment was in connection with the floor prices, which is also explained at great length in my statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I know the explanation, but I do not think it is good. In my opinion the orders in council to which the minister referred did not in any way validate the actions of the millers during the wartime period. That is an opinion, of course, which the minister can attack if he wishes; but to my mind those orders in council have no bearing on the contention made in the McGregor report. As I say, if they have, I cannot understand why the point was not made during the investigation, and why under those circumstances the report would have been made, knowing the careful way in which

the commissioner under the combines act has always proceeded in regard to these matters. Moreover, as the hon. member for Vancouver East suggests to me, Mr. McGregor was one of the enforcement officers during the war, and he would have known of this arrangement when finalized and would have understood the implications of the orders in council. Consequently I do not think the argument advanced in rebuttal of the charges is good or valid.	.
I am not going to thresh old straw. We have had a long debate; and when the people of the country read it, so far as they are able to do so they will have to draw their own conclusions. I am satisfied the government was wrong in withholding the report. I am satisfied that the commissioner acted in good faith; that he made a report which was warranted, and that his recommendation that prosecution should follow was entirely justified on the basis of the evidence placed before him. If the millers had any reason to give as to why they should be granted immunity, I cannot understand why that reason or that evidence was not given to the investigators.
The minister said yesterday that if somebody came and wanted to see documents and so on in an office, the natural thing would be to see that anything which might have a bearing on a subsequent lawsuit would be to some extent protected. Well, I think if any evidence could have been produced to show that they were given privilege or immunity, they would have produced it, because that would have saved a great deal of public discussion and removed any possibility of the industry being under a cloud, apart altogether from protection against attack in the courts when the report was made. Indeed, it would have obviated the necessity for making any report at all.
That is all I want to say at this stage. I shall have some suggestions to make later, because I believe the act needs expansion so that certain other services and so on may be included within its scope. So far as I am concerned, however, the evidence that has been produced and the discussion that has taken place here should enable parliament and the people of Canada to form a considered judgment and conclusion on this matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have not made any comments on the explanation of the Minister of Justice in his extended review of the situation, but I think this is an appropriate point at which to make those comments, since they bear on the question in the minds of hon. members as to the effectiveness of the amendment proposed in section 1 of this bill.

There was a short discussion yesterday during which the minister explained that the amendment contained in section 1, which provides that the Attorney General of Canada may institute and conduct any prosecution or other proceedings under this act, is really only a statement in statutory form of what already exists de facto, and that the existing provision of the combines act which leaves prosecutions under the Criminal Code exclusively to the attorneys general of the provinces has not in fact deprived the Attorney General of Canada of effective power to proceed with actions under both the code and the combines act by the process of consultation and co-operation with the attorneys general of the provinces. In effect that is a correct interpretation of the present situation.
I do suggest, however, that there is another reason why hon. members should feel they cannot pass this section. It is true that a law of this kind does not name individuals, and does not provide that a particular attorney general may do a particular thing; but the effect of this amendment will be that the present attorney general will be able to prosecute under the combines act with a degree of authority which he does not now possess. I think hon. members of this house should question whether the present attorney general, no matter what his motives may have been, has given any good reason for our believing that the act will be strengthened and not weakened if he has a wider measure of authority for prosecution than he now has. It is because of the wider powers that, in form at any rate, he would acquire under this amendment that we must examine the explanation he has given.
The Minister of Justice quite properly took adequate time to review the whole sequence of events which have brought us up to this position. In that review he had full opportunity to explain every detail of the course which has been followed from December 29 last until today. I submit, Mr. Chairman, there is not one word in that explanation which gives any reason whatever for the failure to publish this report in accordance with the act. From the point of view of the relationship of the position between the Minister of Justice and parliament, the regrettable thing is that nowhere in his explanation has the minister indicated any recognition of the gravity of the offence to parliament and to our system in this country. Moreover, I submit there has been a regrettable absence on the part of any member who ordinarily supports the government of any evidence of recognition of the effect of a proceeding of this kind upon the reliance of members of 45781-1381
Combines Investigation Act parliament upon statements given to the house by the Minister of Justice or other members of the government.
In effect, what is the explanation? The Minister of Justice quite reasonably explains that he was in Winnipeg until the third of January, and that on coming to Ottawa he was confronted with an accumulation of problems which required his attention before the opening of parliament a short time later. He quite reasonably explains it was not possible for him to devote the time that he otherwise might have devoted to a reading of this report, and for that reason-it is a valid reason-the time set out in the act for publication passed. I do not think there is a single member of this house who would not accept the explanation of the Minister of Justice about the difficulties he encountered at that time. I do not think there is a single member of this house who would raise any serious question if there had been a delay in publication resulting from a situation of that kind. I do not believe any member would challenge the minister's explanation if he said: I was confronted with these problems. These are difficulties that every member, particularly one who has had cabinet responsibility, will understand. The minister could have said: I am simply stating that under the pressure of business I did delay publication so that I might have an opportunity of examining this report before publication, with the consequent effects that it might have, because as Minister of Justice I felt that when the report was released I should be in a position to make some statement as to the attitude of the government in regard to it. All that is so reasonable, and so much in accordance with the difficulties all of us encounter day by day in meeting our own tasks that no member would have been unreasonable in that respect.
That explanation, however, does not for one moment explain a ten months' delay. It does not for one moment explain the delay in publication until a date which made it impossible for any prosecution to be undertaken. I submit that is one of the very serious aspects of what has developed. It does not reveal why the explanation that has been given to the house on this occasion was not given to the house when parliament was meeting from January until April. No explanation that the Minister of Justice has given suggests for a moment that the same views in regard to the publication of this report were not present in the minds of the cabinet members and in his own mind at that time.
On the contrary, at the time this report first came to his attention he was aware of the effect of its contents. He discussed it

There is nothing, Mr. Chairman, in section 3 which has any bearing whatever on the attempts which the minister explains


he was making to bring some measure of harmony and understanding between the senior government officials who were dealing with this matter, because the difficulty encountered in the presentation of evidence was all disclosed, not only when the Ontario court of appeal gave its judgment, but, long before that, in the trial judgment as well. Hence the difficulty about presentation of evidence and proof as to the association of certain officials and certain documents with what had taken place was clearly in the mind of the government; and if that is the heart of the bill, then there is no reason why this bill was not presented to parliament last spring, with the explanation which has now been given and with the opportunity which then would have been available to this house to express its views at a time when action might still have been taken, if action was deemed appropriate.
Moreover, I am inclined to think that the problem which the amendments proposed in section 3 seek to cover is not so much a problem of new rules of evidence as it is of the presentation of evidence. A careful examination of what took place in the dental case will disclose that without much difficulty the evidence could have been given which would have connected the appropriate documents and individuals with the alleged combine. In making this statement I am directing no criticism to those who handled the case. It would appear either that they were instructed or that they held certain views which in effect prevented judgment in this case.
I come back to this argument: If the meat of the bill now before us is merely an amendment as to rules of evidence and the establishment of association with an alleged combine in cases of this kind, then there is no explanation for this delay; because we did not need to wait until now for the presentation of this simple provision as to how evidence can be brought in that will be effective. These rules as to evidence can have no conceivable bearing upon the appropriateness or otherwise of publication of the report on the alleged milling combine.
I hesitate to say this, Mr. Chairman, because the Minister of Justice has sought to explain the details. But after all, this is the high court of parliament, and it is the duty of every one of us to state what he believes to be the obligation of each minister, of the government as a whole, or of individual members within this high court of parliament. The fact that we may make statements that are in themselves extremely critical or that imply grave concern about the position of any individual within this parliament, is

no more a personal matter than is the necessary statement by a judge or the necessary action by a jury in our courts because it is their duty not to allow personal feelings to restrain appropriate action or to call for action or for statements which would be unjust or inappropriate. It is our duty to state the position as we see it in the light of our understanding of the responsibility to parliament of the government and of individual ministers. In this light, Mr. Chairman, I can only say that the explanation given by the Minister of Justice makes the case infinitely worse than it was before he made it.
Let us come down to what the minister now tells us. He says that the core of the oill before us is merely a provision for more effective proof of certain documents and the more effective establishing of the responsibility of individuals to an association of this kind. If that is so, then by no stretch of the imagination does this amending bill offer the slightest explanation of the minister's failure to comply with the law when he could reasonably have done so, having regard to the difficulties he has explained as to his arrival here on January 3 with an accumulation of work before him. On the contrary, he has given to the commissioner, for his failing to act under the Combines Investigation Act, an explanation which, in the face of this bill and his present statement, simply does not hold water, and in itself challenges our opportunity to place full reliance on the explanations he has given.
Let us see what section 1 does. It is section 1 that we are discussing; the reference to section 3 arose out of the minister's explanation that it was the real core of this amending act.
Section 1 says that the Attorney General of Canada may institute and conduct any prosecution. It is so easy to forget that our established customs may be weakened, step by step, without full recognition of what is happening. Why should the attorney general, and particularly this attorney general, have wider powers and wider discretion when the discretion he has exercised in this case was a discretion not to prosecute without following the ordinary provisions of the act in regard to publication at the time? Everything that has been placed before the House of Commons is an argument why the present attorney general should have no greater responsibilities, but rather infinitely fewer. Every explanation that has been given is one which denies to the present attorney general that wider discretion implied by this amendment, even if it is only placing in statutory form what already exists de facto.
Combines Investigation Act
The explanation given by the Minister of Justice is a long one which seeks to justify the breach of law by the government itself. One of the explanations which I think should be given full attention is that there were changes in the report after January 14, by which time the report should have been published under the act. The minister speaks of different amendments. Mr. Chairman, this explanation is not one which can inspire confidence in the house in connection with any explanations given by the Minister of Justice concerning his responsibilities. The minister, and everyone who has had practical experience in dealing with reports of this kind, knows exactly what may happen under circumstances of the kind. I will go so far as to say that one member of the house particularly, who has had some judicial experience, knows of similar situations in connection with judgments of courts. While a judgment is held up and while a report under any statute is not presented, either a judge or an official will constantly refine and perhaps improve the wording. On rereading he may say to himself that a particular sentence does not express, quite as clearly as it might have, the opinion he had wished to express. He will change that sentence.
It must be remembered that the minister has told us that an effort was being made to bridge the gap which existed between the opinions of certain senior officials who carried on their responsibilities in different departments of government. It may well be -and I imagine it is so-that the commissioner under the combines act, while not in any way varying the sense of the report, sought to give an explanation which would leave no doubt as to what his opinion was in law concerning some of the discussions which had taken place. And that, I submit, Mr. Chairman, was a perfectly proper course, right up to the date the report was published. But it offers no explanation of the failure to publish the report; because we have the statement of the minister that he received a memorandum from the commissioner in January indicating to him when the report should be published. The evidence before us is conclusive that the commissioner felt all along that the report should be published. The withholding of the publication had no relationship in the commissioner's mind at any time to the minor amendments that were made.
So far as the present bill is concerned, I wish to leave no doubt as to our position in regard to the Combines Investigation Act. We believe that it is necessary legislation,

Combines Investigation Act . and that it should be strengthened and clarified. We believe that it should be strengthened from the point of view of effective prosecution, and we believe that every provision in the act must be adhered to by the government of the day and the members of that government-particularly the minister charged with ultimate responsibility under the act.
We believe also that the act should provide a mechanism which will prevent abuses, but at the same time not interfere with those associations which are not injurious to the public interest. That was the purpose intended to be included in the act under the provision that in order to constitute an offence under the act there must be a combine contrary to the public interest. We believe a much more effective way of handling this can be provided. We believe, in other words, that these amendments are inadequate. If the motion to refer the subject matter of the bill to a committee had been adopted-and I am not debating the decision in that respect-there would have been an opportunity to examine fully that point, and to make recommendations. At this stage, in the debate on the bill, it is impossible to provide for adequate amendments which would really make the act effective.
It may well be that some who are discussing the combines act may have different views as to its purposes. I really doubt if there are the differences of views which have been suggested. I believe it is immensely important that combines which are contrary to the public interest should be dealt with effectively. I believe that legislation-and effective legislation-of this kind is essential to the very type of the free competitive system in which I believe.
I am convinced that our idea as to the advantages of free competition is premised on the fact that there will not be a denial of competition by agreements between companies which have the effect of preventing improvement in quality, improvement in usefulness, and reduction in prices by competition. Failure to have an act of this kind which is really effective, and administered effectively by the government in office, is in itself an invitation to that very rigid type of economy with which I disagree, and with which I am sure most members in the house disagree.
Sometimes these discussions are related to a misunderstanding of definitions. I was interested this morning to hear a reference to competition, and the necessity for competition to keep prices down. That is what we believe in. When we talk about a free

economy and free enterprise, we are asserting our belief that the individual man or woman in his or her home in this country benefits most from a system which by competition itself will improve quality and lower prices.
That has been the advantage of this system; and it is because of that system that we have on this continent today the highest standard to be found anywhere in the world. It is because we want to continue that system, to continue that competition and to continue the improvement of the living conditions which come from lowered prices, improved quality and improved usefulness, that we so strongly insist upon an effective act to prevent combines which would destroy competition and which are contrary to the interests of the people of Canada. That is why we are devoting so much attention to what has happened in this particular case and expressing such strong opinions about it.
The Minister of Justice was asked if he would give the assurance that under no circumstances in the future would there be a similar breach of the law-again with that detachment which it is our duty as members of this high court of parliament to observe. The minister's explanation yesterday in that respect was the most cynical statement I have heard since I came into the house early this year, and I regret that there have been a number of them. The minister did not say to the hon. member who asked him the question: I recognize the enormity of a breach by the Minister of Justice of the laws of parliament which every citizen is compelled to observe, and it will not recur. He did not say that. He said in effect-I do not pretend to give the exact words, but I trust he will not question my interpretation: The hon. member who has raised the question places a very low estimate on my intelligence if he thinks that I would let myself in for this much trouble again. That is what he said. I am sure the minister will not suggest that I have misinterpreted his reply. In other words, what he says is this: If we keep it dark, we will really keep it dark this time and will not make this mistake once more.

I had nothing to do with it at all. About anything that is done while I am Minister of Justice I will be kept informed as it goes along. When the time comes that a future report comes down, I hope to have a fairly intelligent view of what the report is concerned with and its nature. This fifteen day period, which is altogether too short a time for anyone to know what he is publishing if he has never seen the report before, can be complied with only if the minister has been in the department beforehand and has some idea of how the investigation has proceeded, what it has dealt with, and so on.
The duty of conducting the investigation and making a report is by statute entirely upon the commissioner, but there is nothing in any part of the set-up which prevents the commissioner from conferring with his minister. If a minister is to avoid difficulty of this sort he should, at the time the report comes in, have a better grasp of the situation which is being dealt with than any minister could possibly have if he is new to the office.

I am definitely convinced that what the minister has just said to this committee demonstrates that far from recognizing the seriousness of what has happened-and I cannot overemphasize my own realization of that seriousness- the minister really thinks it would be a good thing if embarrassment of that kind could be avoided; and I cannot see any evidence that he has any other thought on the subject.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I have no desire not to co-operate in any way possible, but I would know in advance that any memorandum I might prepare would not be acceptable; therefore I will save my time in preparing it and the time of the minister in reading it. Perhaps what I would prepare would have some relation to what I find in one of the many editorials that have been written dealing with this subject. I do not think I have seen the core of the really serious aspects of this matter more clearly brought into focus than they are in an editorial appearing in Toronto Saturday Night of November 22-a highly responsible publication which has not at any time indicated partiality against the government in its discussion of public affairs. After a review of

certain events under the heading "Lawbreaking ministers", I find this in the issue to which I refer:
It is a most dangerous attitude and one which, if allowed to go unrebuked, will extend eventually to even more important matters, if that be possible.
That the report was unjust to the milling industry, and that the government would have been ill-advised to take action upon it, is in our opinion entirely true, but has nothing to do with the case. The law does not say that the government may suppress any report by the commissioner which causes it uneasiness, or with which it disagrees, or which it thinks likely to cause undue agitation in the public mind. The law says that the reports of the commissioner shall be made public within fifteen days; and the whole object of that provision was, as our Ottawa correspondent pointed out last week, to put the reports beyond the reach of any possible political pressures.
In the United Kingdom, we do not hesitate to state, the unearthing of a situation such as this would lead to the resignation of at least the minister chiefly concerned. If the political atmosphere of Canada were as healthy as that of- the United Kingdom-if electors demanded the same standards of their responsible rulers, and if rulers had the same sense of obligation to parliament and to the country-the same result would follow here.
This is not an overstatement of the seriousness of the situation with which we are confronted, and the attitude of the minister. If the minister had said: I came to Ottawa only on January 3; the report had been presented on December 29, and I remained in the west to clean up certain details; when I came here I was confronted with the necessity of preparing for parliament and I was not able to attend to this for a while; as Minister of Justice I have no discretion in regard to publication, but I did want to know something of what it was about; therefore, there was some delay which I regret. If this had been said, every hon. member would have agreed that we could not be critical of so reasonable a position. This default is continued, however, and when the explanation is given it is clear that the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not want the report published, and the Minister of Justice was not prepared to create an issue such as would have resulted, under our system, in the resignation of the minister. That is the situation.
Instead, however, the minister comes here and says he is assuming the responsibility. This morning he says, in effect, that a thing of this kind will not happen again; remember that on this occasion I did not have an opportunity of reading the report before publication. Why should he, unless he believes he should have an opportunity of reading it before it is in final form? What does that mean? Is there any hon. member who can misinterpret what the minister has in mind, that the report should toe the subject of discussion before it is published? The purpose of publication was stated by the one who
Combines Investigation Act moved in this house the insertion of that section of the act, Mr. Mackenzie King. In his explanation of the purpose, he emphasized the prophylactic power of publication, and the independence of the officials in carrying out what they thought to be the necessary exposure of the conditions they had found, without the intervention of the government or any member of the government. That was the intention of this idea of publication. I believe it should be carried out.
I could easily put into the minister's mouth words in the form of verse which do seem to sum up his attitude. He will find them in Gilbert and Sullivan's "Iolanthe":
The law Is the true embodiment Of everything that's excellent.
It has no kind of fault or flaw,
And I, my lords, embody the law.
In other words, never mind what parliament has passed; never mind what the responsibility is under the acts that those elected by the people pass; if we think anything might result from this with which we do not agree, then we will assume the responsibility as members of the government for changing the law, in effect if not in actual words.
I heard a comment a moment ago about quoting Gilbert and Sullivan which was not loud enough for the reporter to hear. As a matter of fact, Gilbert and Sullivan might well be quoted in respect to certain aspects of this matter. There is another reference to Gilbert and Sullivan which might be applied to another minister. I believe he well occupies the role of Pooh-Bah in another famous play which perhaps is better known than "Iolanthe". Nevertheless the fact that the ministerial Pooh-Bah is running not only his own department but the Department of Justice as well is no explanation for the Minister of Justice waiting ten months to get on his feet and resist that overriding power, with the qualifications he made, as soon as he had found out what it was all about.
For ten months, the government has been in contempt, and deliberate contempt, of parliament. The longer the explanations are that are put before us, the more it is emphasized why this government still thinks it had the right to break the law under the circumstances which existed at that time. If that explanation is sound, then it applies to other responsibilities of the government. If that explanation is sound, we have no way of knowing whether there are any other reports that should have been made or any other things this government should have done which it has failed to do under the

Combines Investigation Act same comfortable doctrine. It strikes at the very root of our system of responsible government.
I think it is time for us to recognize, Mr. Chairman, as has unfortunately been recognized too late in some other countries, that the first line of defence of our free society is not the Oder or the Rhine, but is right here in parliament. The first place for us to defend our free society and our system is the place where that freedom can find its guarantee, if the full responsibility of parliament is exercised as it was intended to be exercised.
If the present explanation is accepted, there is no assurance that this intolerable situation is any nearer an end than it was when this default was exposed so reluctantly. Who will forget the incident when the Minister of Justice was prepared to table the correspondence and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said, "No, no."

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to prolong the debate unnecessarily,, but in view of some of the remarks of hon. members in the opposition I feel it my duty, both as a member of the Canadian reserve army and as a member of parliament, to correct some of the impressions which have been given.
First I want to congratulate the minister upon the able way in which he has presented the report of his department to the committee. The minister is also to be congratulated upon having the courage of his convictions in asking for an investigation into the affairs of the Canadian navy, and for his subsequent publishing of Admiral Mainguy's report in full. I intend to leave the high-sounding philosophy on the theory of defence to the opposition, and to deal with the facts as I see them in relation to the reserve army.
Before the outbreak of the last war we had two armies in Canada, namely the permanent force and the non-permanent active militia. These two forces were governed by the same book, but actually were two distinct forces, with not too much good feeling between them. We had different rules and regulations in regard to training, pay, rations, clothing and equipment. In spite of all this, history has proved that we would not have been able to field the troops we did at the first of the war had it not been for the excellent work done by the N.P.A.M. between the wars.
Today, thanks to the policy laid down by the Minister of National Defence, we have one army. There is a good feeling of comradeship between those in the active force and those in the reserve force. All of us draw the same pay and allowances. We draw the.same rations and wear the same clothing. Our training is the same; and it is the aim of all reservists to become as proficient as those in the active army. Those of us who were in the N.P.A.M. between the wars and are in the reserve army now, are most grateful to those who have laid down this policy and saw to it that it was carried out. The aim of those in the active army, from the top to the bottom, seems to be that of furthering the interests of the reserve army. After all, that is one of the main sources of manpower for Canada's army in the event of war.

However, I think everybody admits that there has been extreme difficulty in getting men into the reserve units. The recruiting campaigns which have been put on have been flops.
In Calgary we have had two or three army weeks that I remember, during which the various units came down town with pieces of their equipment. This equipment was put in prominent places such as busy street corners and so forth to be seen by the people. Posters were put up. Advertisements were put in the newspapers. Talks were given on the radio, and so on, all designed to draw in recruits for both the reserve force and the permanent force. So far as the reserve forces are concerned, these means were just hopeless. Very few recruits were secured as a result of them, in Calgary at any rate. I understand the same thing was true across most of the country.
Speaking on the same day the hon. member for Kamloops said, as reported on page 1695 of Hansard:
If we are to play an effective role in defending our own territories, we must be able to put in the field an effective striking force within weeks or at the most a month of the time of the outbreak of hostilities. Is our reserve force capable of expansion in that way, to fill the role which that picture thrusts upon it? It certainly is not.
A little further on the hon. member said:
If my hon. friend who asked me the question, or any other hon. member who is interested, will take the trouble to consult with the commanding officers of any of our reserve units, he will find the answer to his question. Those officers are reluctantly compelled to say that their units would not be battleworthy for a period not of weeks or a month, but of months or a year. We therefore have not a reserve force capable of taking the field, under present conditions, within less than a year from the outbreak of hostilities.
I quote those examples because they are typical of the criticism which has been levelled against the government and the reserve army. I do not propose to tell the committee what is wrong with other units in Canada; rather I propose to tell hon. members about one unit that has been able to recruit all the soldiers it wanted and to train them efficiently. There certainly are several units in Canada which are outstanding, and what I say in connection with one probably has to do with them all.
I refer to the Eighth Princess Louise's (New Brunswick) Hussars, fifth armoured regiment, with headquarters at Sussex, New Brunswick. Lieutenant Colonel G. R. H. Ross is the officer commanding and I have the honour to be second in command. I shall not go into the history of this regiment except to say that it is a very old unit and had a good war record in the recent war where it served throughout with the fifth Canadian division.

Upon being discharged from the active army in 1946 those members of the overseas unit who were interested were struck off strength to the reserve unit, the second regiment which had carried on during the war. A short summer camp was held in 1946 and I believe we were the only reserve unit in Canada to go into camp that year. The following year the unit trained at Camp Utopia, New Brunswick. In the meantime the four squadron headquarters had been established with A and B squadrons at Sussex, C squadron at Sackville and R.H.Q. at Hampton. This meant that we had personnel spread over a radius of 100 miles, which gave us a number of self-accounting units. This in itself is good training for the personnel concerned.
Recruiting was slow at first but those with the interests of the unit at heart soon developed a system which worked. We had been supplied with sufficient building accommodation for an armoured unit together with tanks and wheeled vehicles. This with the stores required for general military training and an A and T staff gave us enough to make training constructive and interesting. General military training was carried out at local headquarters and all armoured corps training was carried out at Sussex. We found that the recruiting campaigns made people think about the armed services and then all that was required was a little personal contact. Today our unit is within one hundred of being up to strength and we attribute this to the following:
1.	Efficient administration, at all levels.
2.	Well "laid on" progressive training leading to the qualifications of trained soldiers and tradesmen.
3.	Good "Q" management-this includes good meals, sufficient clothing of the right size, regimental badges, flashes, ties, et cetera. All personnel attending week-end schemes or special courses are issued with sheets, pillow slips, pillows, blankets and the barrack rooms are conducted properly.
4.	The social life of the unit. No unit can exist wholly on its social activities, but they are very necessary to maintain a proper level of military life.
All the items just mentioned should be the usual and not the exception. By making military life in the reserve army interesting and constructive, we built up an esprit de corps which, as you all know, is the secret of any unit. I cannot agree with the hon. member from Calgary East that it is hard to get men into the reserve army, nor can I agree that the recruiting campaigns which have been put on were flops. On the contrary we find these recruiting campaigns a great asset.
Supply-National Defence In fact, on checking the records I find that allowing for wastage the strength of the Calgary reserve army units as at October 31, 1949, compared with the strength as at October 31, 1948, shows a net gain of 17-7 per cent. This shows that these advertising campaigns were not a flop in the hon. member's constituency as he suggested.
In my opinion no unit will ever recruit by waiting for the men to come to it. Each man presently on strength has a friend and he in turn has a friend and if the soldier is sufficiently interested he can bring several of his friends into the unit. We can bring our unit up to strength at will, and this will be done during the next recruiting campaign. There are, of course, always a number of non-effectives. In the case of officers and N.C.O.'s they are immediately struck off strength if they do not attend training without having obtained permission to be absent. In the case of other ranks an attempt is made to ascertain why they are not attending and if they persist in not attending, then they too are struck off strength. Of course, personnel can be forced to attend training under the Militia Act, but we do not want anyone on strength who does not want to belong.
In 1944 at the battle of Coriano Ridge, which was one of the battles of the Gothic line, members of the unit came across a badly wounded colt several days old beside her mother which had been killed during the battle. The colt was taken to the M.I.R. and patched up. The colt lived and was taken with the unit as a mascot. Eventually, the mascot went with the unit to northwest Europe and eventually was shipped to Canada. This colt, named Princess Louise, has become a member of the Hampton branch of the Canadian Legion and is also a member of the reserve unit. On all ceremonial parades and guards this mascot leads the parade. This unit put on guards of honour for both Viscount Alexander and Field Marshal Montgomery, and Princess Louise formed part of each parade. The presence of this mascot has helped to build morale within the unit and has helped recruiting.
For the past two years we have taken more troops into summer camp than any other unit in Canada and in each case could have taken far more than our allotment. The winter training done at local headquarters and at R.H.Q. trains the soldier for the specialized training he will get at summer camp. The troops enjoy summer camp and there is always a high percentage who would like to remain for additional training.
As you all know, a tank driving range requires a lot of territory, and since the tanks

Supply-National Defence are so heavy it is impossible to transport them around the country without doing permanent damage to certain bridges, and roads. As I mentioned before, all armoured corps training was of necessity carried on at R.H.Q. at Sussex. Each squadron must attend one week end training period per month and one week end is reserved for officers and N.C.O.'s. This is all specialist training, which in the case of other ranks can lead to qualification as tradesmen.
In addition, there are many schemes arranged with other units in the area. Three weeks ago, for instance, there were over 600 personnel quartered in our lines doing a tank-cum-infantry scheme. Last year we put on a tank-cum-infantry scheme with the air force and artillery in support. Two weeks ago we were hosts to the area shoot at which every unit in the New Brunswick area was represented. You can see by this that the attitude toward the reserve army in New Brunswick is very good. In fact, according to figures published in the press recently, the province of New Brunswick had more personnel in the reserve army per capita than any other province in Canada.
An important part of the work of a reserve army is sponsoring cadet corps. We have affiliated with us five cadet corps. These corps are trained under direction of the area cadet officer together with what help we can give them with our own officers and N.C.O.'s and with the A and T staff. The members of these cadet corps are brought into R.H.Q. at least once a year and are given a practical knowledge of tanks and wheeled vehicles on strength. Annually we present a suitably engraved cup to the best affiliated cadet corps. We find that these cadet corps provide a steady stream of recruits for the reserve army.
Our percentage of overseas personnel in the ranks in relation to recruits is rather high. Twenty-two per cent of the other ranks had service with the active force during the recent war. Sixty per cent of the N.C.O.'s and 80 per cent of the officers served with the active force. In my opinion this is exceptionally good, and is of great benefit in training recruits. There are many officers and N.C.O.'s in the area who are fully qualified and yet have been unable to get on strength of a reserve unit because the complement is full. To overcome this, and to give reserve units the advantage of having additional trained officers and N.C.O.'s at their command, the department has allowed us to take on additional personnel from the supplementary reserve officers list up to our war establishment in equivalent ranks. We are also allowed now to take on W.O.'s and N.C.O.'s surplus to establishment up to 100 per cent of our war establishment.

The minister has made the statement several times that the 8th P.L. (N.B.) Hussars is the largest and best reserve unit in Canada today. We are very proud of this fact. It is our intention to bring this unit up to strength in the near future, and to maintain its standard of efficiency.
The hon. member for Kamloops made the statement on page 1695 of Hansard for Friday, November 11, that if we take any year from 1924 to 1938 or 1939, we shall find that the size of the reserve army is substantially in excess of the reserve army today. Although the reserve army strength before the last war was higher than it is today, nevertheless this was to some extent a paper strength, for we were training only 64-4 per cent of our total strength at that time, while we have been training an average of 86-4 per cent over the last four years. As a matter of fact, last year was one of our best years when we were training 92 [DOT] 2 per cent of the reserve army. Training today, compared with that between the wars, is so far superior that figures do not tell the truth. We are actually training today with sufficient men, equipment and buildings, together with good training at summer camps and summer schools. The men are really efficient, and many of them are ready to take the field, whereas between the wars, as we all know, training was of very little value.
Those of us who were in the N.P.A.M. between the wars remember well the conditions under which we trained. I personally remember when all ranks contributed their pay to regimental funds in order that we could hire horses and pay expenses to go into camp. When we were formed into an armoured unit around 1938, we were not allowed to train sufficient personnel, although we did get some money for the hire of cars which we used in lieu of tanks. In 1939, a few months before war broke out, we took into camp our authorized training allotment of fifty-five all ranks. I want to impress on all hon. members again that this was only a few months before war broke out. These conditions do not exist today. We have sufficient equipment and are allowed to take into camp enough personnel to assure a high standard of training in the reserve army.
At the present time I do not feel that Canada needs or can afford a large standing army. There is only one source of money, and that is the Canadian taxpayer. If the money is spent on defence it is not available for the many other needs of the country. There is sufficient money allotted to the reserve army today to train it efficiently. Some members of the opposition have voiced the fear that this money is being wasted.

I know that it is not being wasted in my own unit, and I cannot entertain the fears expressed by so many of the opposition that we could not recruit quickly enough today in the event of hostilities breaking out. I was in Toronto the other night at the royal winter fair, and there was a guard of honour put on by the reserve army. I think it indicated the state of training of a good many of the units of the reserve army. The Irish regiment of Canada from Toronto provided the guard of honour for the vice-regal party, and it was exceptionally well done. I think they should be highly praised for their efforts.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I feel that if my own unit, together with several other units in Canada, can accomplish what we have under the existing regulations there should be no reason why other units cannot do equally well. It shows there is nothing wrong with our system, and we know by experience that we have sufficient equipment and material to make the program a success. There are local conditions which affect each unit differently, but surely these can be overcome by those who so successfully overcame the obstacles presented to them in the last war. To those who doubt the efficiency of the training being carried out in both the active and reserve army, I suggest that they arrange with the minister to visit units so that they can see for themselves the efficient way in which the program is being carried out.
By comparison with the N.P.A.M., and having in mind the success which we had in mobilizing the forces at the outbreak of the last war, I am convinced that we are in a far better position than ever before in the history of this country, and that we could mobilize our forces today quickly enough to take care of any emergency.
