My suggestions are not made in criticism of what the minister has been doing, far from it. They are suggestions with which I think he will agree once they are presented to him. I am not a military man, but I have seen a great deal of the good work which the department has done. First of all I should like to refer to the book which the department has brought out covering many phases of its activities. One of the matters referred to in it is the union of the services. The United States have had the same trouble. You may remember after the Pearl Harbor disaster, and after the close of the war, they had the same trouble under two or three of
Supply-National Defence their leaders. They tried to unite into one organization the army, navy, air force and other services. We saw what happened there. Since that time there have been effected some changes which have been brought about by the new conditions now existing.
I want to call attention to a book by Lord Vansittart entitled "Lessons of my Life". He was the British ambassador to Germany for fifteen years. In his book he warns the world about the disaster that is surely coming between the east and the west. I say the minister would be well advised to ponder, hearken and listen to what the ambassador has said because he has offered some good constructive advice along these lines. In Everybody's Weekly of November 12, 1949, Lord Vansittart has called attention to the grave danger awaiting the world arising out of our association with the Soviet union, which never intends to carry out anything it proposes.
This is a very important matter. Here we have a representative of the United States and a representative of Britain conferring, with whom? They are conferring with the representatives of the Soviet. The picture shows Mr. Bevin of Britain and Mr. Dean Acheson of the United States enjoying a jest with Mr. Vishinsky of the U.S.S.R.; but the legend under the picture says, "but the time has come to cease 'smarming' Soviet representatives." The heading of the article is "Stop this foolishness" and beneath it is this statement:
Only fools play cards with notorious sharpers, yet our government continues to make worthless "agreements" with the communist states which are bent on our destruction.
That is exactly correct; and in the article Lord Vansittart goes on to say:
It is remarkable that the democracies still cannot really wake up to the true nature and intentions of the communist conspiracy. There have been encouraging signs in the United States and Australia, where some of the conspirators have been convicted and sentenced, but in the main the democracies go on blindly and softly preaching and practising "liberty to destroy liberty."
This was the line taken by the German republic towards nazism and by Czechoslovakia towards communism. In both cases-and in others also-the totalitarian system enslaved the people; yet we still will not learn the lesson that all these insidious and despotic systems are deadly poison, and that all their advocates should be regarded in that light.
Thus foolishly looking upon communism as a party instead of a conspiracy, the democracies- governments and peoples-always begin to recoil from effective action at the very moment when they begin to nerve themselves for it. Consequently, communism continues to enjoy wholly unreasonable facilities for carrying on its destructive work; and though it sometimes suffers minor setbacks-as in Greece-broadly speaking it is gaining ground, and democracy is losing it.

Supply-National Defence
Then the article goes on to describe where the landslide began. Hon. members may remember that the other day, speaking in a debate on defence, Mr. Churchill said the Soviet were invited to take part in the Pacific war just before the collapse of Japan, and he had not consented to it. He also said that instead of the western allies going right on into Berlin, which they could have captured, they halted a few miles away, at Stressen, and as a result brought about the situation we have seen in Berlin since the end of the war. I need not take time to read Mr. Churchill's speech, but he pointed out that the Russians were invited to join in the war against Japan by the late President Roosevelt and by General Eisenhower, and they came into the Pacific though that had been the preserve of the British and American armies. What did they do there, just three days later? Japan was about to collapse, anyway; but they landed five hundred thousand men in Manchuria about a week before the end of the Japanese war, and finally overran the whole of China, just as they have overrun about three-quarters of Asia.	Burma, Malaya, and many other
countries in Asia are gone, and there is very little left.
Then Lord Vansittart went on to say:
Briefly, we must "recognize" communism everywhere, not in the old diplomatic sense but in the modern one-as our inevitable foe. This attitude should be practised not only by democratic governments but by all democratic individuals. For example, British ministers should limit their attendance at communist feasts and festivals to the barest minimum, and should never be photographed shaking hands with, and grimacing at, communist politicians, diplomatists, or other treacherous agents. This smarming only misleads our own people. Truth requires a stern face; let our rulers wear it.
All this involves a break with past habits, procedures and traditions; but I have long said that we must revolutionize our own outlook, if we are to cope with the attempt at world-wide revolution which now threatens to engulf freedom. The enemy is at our doors-and within them. Why not hit him in time?
I believe that is the truth coming from a man who has had the greatest experience. He goes on:
I came early to the conclusion that nazism meant war, and coined the phrase "Keep Germany lean."
He goes on to point out that there is the same grave danger of Germany rising again. He was ambassador there for fifteen years, and he knows the people. He warns the nations of the world that Germany may yet rise and be restored as a great industrial and economic nation, and eventually cause a third war. The other day I mentioned these slave camps that are all over Europe. Here is the picture of a map of eastern Europe with the slave camps dotted all over it. There
(Mr. Church.]
are millions of slaves in these places in the Soviet, the satellite countries of the Balkans and the Far East. All those countries are as much afraid of Germany rising again as they are of the Soviet nation, and we should be aware of that danger also.
Lord Vansittart goes on to say:
We must revise our former definition of diplomacy. It no longer exists to ensure good relations. The missions of the iron curtain exist everywhere to foster bad relations by promoting subversion and preparing sabotage. Diplomacy therefore no longer consists in drafting treaties, which communists always break even when they have signed them. All that we get by trying to compromise with evil is first a series of unwarrantable humiliations, and then some waste paper.
This has been the course and outcome of every agreement that we have ever made with the Kremlin, and in particular of the so-called peace treaties with its satellites. We are reduced to constant protests that solemn pledges are being violated in every particular; and in return we receive an insolent smack in the face with Russia's open approval. Why continue to play cards with notorious sharpers? If we ask to be cheated, we must not grumble if we are gratified.
Let us drop all this, and on no account even try to conclude a treaty with this Russia about this Germany.
Nothing of this sort is possible, since it is the Soviet intention to dominate all Germany. We should, on the contrary, make our own arrangements with western Germany, regardless of any communist splutters.
Similarly the democratic powers should make their own treaty with Japan, irrespective of Soviet obstruction. Russia can sign or stay out. I prefer the latter. Yet when the American Secretary of State was recently asked what we would do if the Kremlin pursued its wrecking tactics, he replied that we had not thought about that yet. It is high time that we did.
Russian prestige has been badly rattled by the election of Yugoslavia to the security council, despite Vishinsky's threats. The ingenuities of our diplomacy should henceforth be bent to shake it still further-not to handclasps and negotiations. Communism is groggy in many parts of its empire; and we have many openings for weakening it, particularly on the economic side.
Moscow has bitten off more than it can chew. It cannot supply its slave states, which must consequently look west for machinery and raw materials. Do not let us help them out of their troubles. We need not, of course, break off trade relations altogether; but we should be careful to do nothing which might enable communism to cover up its commercial inefficiencies. The greater its troubles the greater its loss of face everywhere, and the greater, accordingly, the possibility of eventually liberating the oppressed.
Communism insists on 100 per cent servility to the Kremlin of all its members. This caused Tito to kick, and his gesture created a crack throughout eastern Europe. There is no Titoism in China, but we might help to bring it about by a policy which would ensure that communism cannot live up to its promises, or even extricate itself from its dilemmas.
Now, that is the gospel truth. There are three or four other matters to which I wish to refer. I am glad to see that the minister has followed the practice of the United States in issuing a booklet on national defence. I have in my hand the annual report of the

Secretary of the United States' Navy, issued by John L. Sullivan. There was a John L. Sullivan who was a champion boxer in earlier times. This booklet sells for thirty cents and is published in many languages. It gives an account of the efficiency of the navy, and is divided into subjects such as aircraft, ammunition, appropriations, atomic energy, chief of naval operations, cold-weather operations, and construction. There are references to many other matters such as the marine corps, what they are doing, fiscal administration and all that kind of thing. It lists the various departments such as the medical service, the naval stations, the national military establishments. I am glad to see that our minister has issued a similar booklet containing a multitude of matters, and dealing with civil defence.
At this point, I wish to thank the minister for giving the opposition a chance to bring these matters to the attention of the house under item 250. It is of course,-Mr. Amery says in the National Review-always open to Canada to become absorbed into the American economy. No doubt that would add to the balanced expansion of the North American continent as a whole. The greater part of the expansion would, however, by the sheer scale and momentum of the United States economy, continue to take place south of the frontier. Statesmen like Sir John A. Macdonald, with his insistence on Canadian east and west development and on effective protection against the United States, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with his bold initiative in establishing unilateral preference to Britain, foresaw the meaning of Canada's position and of its opportunities. Today these opportunities are far greater. Canada has reached a point in her development when she should take a leading part in the development of the British commonwealth, as well as in the regeneration of Europe, if she but willed it. In Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Amery well says, she has a Prime Minister with an undisputed majority in parliament and an even more complete hold over French Canada. He has already shown his initiative and originality of outlook in connection with the Atlantic pact, and in his insistence on regional policies. Is it inconceivable that, like Sir Wilfrid Laurier before him, he might take a bold step that would help to loosen the present log jam in the world's economy?
The greatest obstacle to such a move in the direction of building up Canada's position as a leading member in an economic group more than capable of matching the United States is really psychological. I believe that is correct.
I should like myself to see some action taken towards the establishment of a Pacific
Supply-National Defence pact, since the Pacific is the back door into Canada, whereas the Atlantic is at our front door. The Atlantic pact involves about 200 million people, but in the Pacific area there are six or seven hundred million, if southern China were included. Some action should be taken immediately against communist Russia, which has met its match in the west but which is now out of control in the east. In 1938 I called the attention of the house to the fact that from Puget sound to the southern Queen Charlotte islands there are nearly 700 miles of unprotected coast line, and it was only by a miracle that Canada escaped direct invasion after Pearl Harbor.
Canada should take some action to control the east and stop communist Russia from controlling Asia. The Atlantic pact and the Marshall plan discourage the communists in the Atlantic region, but let us not forget that unless we have a Pacific pact all we do at our front door will be of little effect. It will not prevent Russia from overrunning the Far East. There must be a considered plan backed by economic support from the countries that are involved in the Pacific.
General MacArthur has done good work in the Far East, and the United States should take the lead in establishing a Pacific pact. In these modern days when bandits and burglars are so busy in our large cities, one must not forget to lock the back door as well as the front door, and we should remind ourselves that the same condition prevails in considering the possibility of warfare in the Atlantic and Pacific today.
What are Canada's defence measures, even after the signing of this Atlantic pact, and does the signing of that pact give us security in case of a third war? In this debate, I have a right to ask the government to give to the house and the country an assurance that all proper means will be taken to see that our armed forces are prepared with effective plans on land and sea and in the air, for the defence of our country. This should include the re-establishment of the air training plan in Canada, and if it is deemed necessary, such home defence measures as the setting up of a home guard. I am far from satisfied that Canada has real security today, and I am free to admit that so far as our defence forces are concerned we are like Ethelred the Unready. As I said in the debate on foreign affairs on July 26, 1948, there is no use pretending we have any adequate security today. I request the government to give us a clear statement as to what additional security the Atlantic treaty gives us.
For some time after 1945 and for about two years after Mr. Churchill's speech at Fulton, nothing was done to arouse the

Supply-National Defence Atlantic countries to the real situation. Communism was like an unsuspected cancer and its ravages went unheeded. Since last fall the western democracies have become wide awake to the grave weaponless war Russia is waging and they are aware of the grave danger.
Canada has worked with Russia as a neutral, as an enemy, and as an ally, and has done so on three occasions. The first was in 1935, when Hitler was beginning to show Germany and the world the fear of a second war; Mr. Eden went to Moscow and achieved a triumph-previously he had gone to France, Italy and the Balkans-in the matter of a union that included Russia. Mr. Eden, then Lord Privy Seal, was met at the railway station in Moscow by Mr. Litvinoff and also by the British ambassador; and at a dinner given by Russia Stalin drank the health of Great Britain, and the party went to the theatre after.
The second time was in 1941 after Hitler attacked Russia and Russia was welcomed by Mr. Churchill as an ally; and on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the founding of the Soviet republic a celebration was held in London and the Archbishop of Canterbury prayed for the victory of the Russian army.
The third time of unity was at San Francisco and both the east and west united in the formation of the UNO to promote peace. Why then do they not allow the allies to get behind the iron curtain and to see what is going on there?
I would call the last three years the weaponless war; for the world now, thanks to Russia, is faced with two kinds of warfare. As the atom bomb has been perfected by the United States, the Soviet union has deserved a more powerful treatment. In the cold, brazen, weaponless war-and she conquers without destruction by this method of warfare-ten countries have been scuttled under, and behind the iron curtain others are almost under the shadow of aggression; the entire world is kept in restless fear of destruction. It is something new in warfare, this struggle for survival, and a challenge is given that armed forces are to maintain any challenge, for war is now waged against us. Unless we win the struggle of Berlin we shall not win the larger struggle. We seem to have failed to appreciate what was involved at Berlin. What was involved there was the command of the sea. That is what the issue was at Berlin. You apparently have lost it; and if you do lose it at Berlin, you are going to lose command of the sea on the Atlantic and the Pacific. Their cold war is only one of camouflage, and has lulled the west into a wrong sense of thinking it has security when it has not.

Never has the House of Commons been faced with graver issues than now. We face the most serious economic disaster, and a very direct military threat, as we go on pretending that we have security. We also err, as does the United States, in taking Britain's supremacy of the sea for granted. There is only one path to take, and our Ottawa politicians will not follow it, namely empire consolidation, which stood us so well in two long wars. Why is any scheme of internationalism, however absurd, preferred and adopted instead of finding real security with our own family members in the dominions and crown colonies? The United Nations are heading us into what I believe will be a third strife, and the west is now no match for the east. Canada should learn that we should follow our own dominions and crown colonies that saved us in two wars and not depend altogether on Washington, although the United States is a friendly nation. Stalin's Russia is just as dangerous to the peace of the world as was Hitler's Germany and, waging a weaponless war, has already conquered huge areas of Europe and Asia. I find an analogy between the failure of the United States and Britain to occupy Berlin and the failure of Hannibal to enter ancient Rome, and Carthage was afterwards destroyed. I note that 38,000 tons of rubber were exported monthly from Malaya to Russia while Canada and the empire got none. I have given this as my opinion: no more goods or services to these countries behind the iron curtain without some promises accordingly.
The .entry of Russia into the war had rendered the Japanese military position hopeless. The possession of Manchuria was vital to the Japanese war economy; it was impossible to hold Manchuria against the flood of vastly superior Russian armies. The use of the atomic bomb accelerated at most by a couple of weeks or so a surrender which would have been inevitable. But had it been the Japanese who had led the way with this particular weapon, the effects would scarcely have been of greater military importance than the German use of flying bombs and rockets in 1944. There would have been but few of such bombs available; to have used them the Japanese must have dropped them from aircraft. Attempts to bomb vital Anglo-American bases would have come up against a crushing Anglo-American superiority in fighter aircraft plus radar, and other means of defence. Manchuria is a land of immense spaces. An atomic bomb dropped here or there would have been of no particular importance. The Russian armies would have continued to flood Manchuria. The Anglo-Americans would have continued to push forward their

own plans for invasion. The use of atomic bombs by the Japanese would have been a temporary shock but would scarcely have affected the issue or _ its outcome. The very fact that every new means of attack evolves from older means connotes that the older means of defence can be swiftly improved and expanded to meet the new danger. Whether the new means of defence become available in time depends upon us.
I may say that the British commonwealth and empire must depend on its own strength for salvation as a family of nations. The league of nations, the United Nations, a united Europe, or the latest hope, the Marshall offer-none of these can do for the British commonwealth and empire what it must achieve for itself by co-operation, enterprise and the strength of its own right arm. Let us by all means seek co-operation with nations whose interests and outlook are akin to our own, and whose security would be jeopardized if the British empire were the victim of aggression. But let us turn once more to our own kith and kin within our own empire, and rely upon our own character and resources for the working out of our salvation as a family of nations.
The United Nations so far has been a modern tower of Babel. Canada and Great Britain should not allow their interests to be the plaything of the United Nations. You cannot obtain peace by any such agency. No country will ever allow other countries and the United Nations to settle its affairs unless that country is too weak to defend its own interests, as Canada is by our disarmament.
The future of both Canada and the United States depends on their own peoples. We need the closest and the most absolute cooperation, collaboration and understanding between this country and the rest of the British empire and between Canada and the United States. Our position is of great importance. Our air policy, for instance, should be planned in close consultation with Britain, and we should have an empire security council such as has been advocated. We should now re-establish in Canada the empire air training plan as a security measure in days like these, in addition to this Atlantic pact which I support and which I hope will prove successful.
Never has the House of Commons been faced with graver issues than at present. Canada should rearm. It is almost too late to do so. Our motto in Canada should be that of Oliver Cromwell: put your trust in God and keep your powder dry. And we should feature it as it applies at this hour in world affairs, which are so dark. Empty Ottawa platitudes will amount to nothing,
Supply-National Defence as will depending on the UNO at Lake Success for our defence. I do not forget when Hitler overran Sudetenland, and Czechoslovakia and the streets of Prague. Our policy has been to side with the Ottawa government in their disarmament policy, and that of scuttle, quit and haul down the flag on the seven seas. Canada should not do that. I believe the government of the day has a program which no doubt it will carry out. I believe Canada should at once send to Britain a message of hope and a promise for the future. I have tried the past few years to tell the House of Commons that the British at home and overseas are one great family, and we should remember that Mr. Menzies, then prime minister of Australia, when he addressed the members of the Senate and the House of Commons here, stressed that point. As he said recently in Australia:
If the price we pay for this second experiment in universal organization is a weakening of our understanding of the importance of the British empire or a lessening of our implicit devotion to it, then the price we will have paid for the United Nations will be almost as disastrous as the price we almost paid for the League of Nations. Do not misunderstand me in this.
I	am saying that it would be the blunder of our lives if in instinctive loyalty to a new world organization completely experimental and almost completely untried we cast away our ancient loyalty which has been the strength of our lives and the rock upon which our houses have been built.
On June 16 last I expressed the very same thing when discussing the estimates for national defence and foreign affairs. I said there was no use our pretending we had such security. It is difficult to understand a great many of these matters. However that is the position I take.
Fortunately the west can confront Russia with overwhelming strength in industry, munitions and manpower, and has established a lead in atomic research which it will be immensely difficult for the Kremlin to overtake. It is our duty to do all in our power to preserve that lead.
Yet, assuming that a balance of power in our favour is maintained, the question remains: Is this sufficient to enable the world to settle down? Is it conceivable that there can really be a secure and contented world while Russia holds half Europe in thrall? Can genuine peace be established while Europe is half slave and half free? Again, is not more than Europe involved? If Asia, besides China and including India, Burma and the East Indies, comes under the Russian grip, can there be world recovery? These are questions for the second stage of the conflict in which we are all at present engaged. When retreat is forced on Russia somewhere, the scene may brighten everywhere.

Supply-National Defence
The main point to remember about the atomic bomb is that its use may depend on the gradual restoration of a more civilized world. Humanity may have to face the question: Which is the less unendurable, a vast physical destruction, or the surrender of the whole of mankind to a diabolical tyranny such as the world has never seen?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I regret much less not having read the papers recently because the hon. member for Broadview has been generous enough to give us the benefit of his reading. He made a most interesting speech which I shall send tomorrow to the military experts who are in town, especially to Sir William Slim, British chief of staff. It is important for them to know what is being said in the House of Commons on the subjects of military and external affairs.
I am not going to make a long speech, because everything that could be said about defence matters has been said by some experts whom I see in front of me. I give credit to the minister and his immediate predecessor for having done so well with the Department of National Defence, after all that had happened before. I wish them success.
I cannot do otherwise, however, than make a few observations which came to my mind some years ago, and particularly in November 1944 when the question of conscription was debated. At that time the late minister of national defence, the one who had resigned on the conscription issue, said that there were some weaknesses in the Canadian army in France. This was broadcast throughout the country and the world. Not long afterwards the German offensive thrust to the south causing the death of many soldiers in the American and Canadian armies.
I have often wondered if it would not be better to discuss questions of defence in camera. Expenditures might be mentioned in the house, because they are of interest to the public; but what does the average citizen know about defence? There are some military experts and some civilian experts who have studied the matter; but many people may be under the wrong impression. If defence matters were discussed in camera every one would have a full opportunity to say all he has to say without endangering the security of the country.
Some hon. members may say that would not be democratic. During the war some secret sittings of the house were held to discuss matters of defence, and they brought good results. Not long ago I saw two articles

which appeared in Maclean's magazine referring to the U-boats which came up the St. Lawrence river. At the time it happened there was difficulty in calling a secret sitting, because the then prime minister and the then minister of national defence objected. After some discussion however they agreed to have a few secret sittings, which served a useful purpose.
I submit this not only to the Minister of National Defence but to all my colleagues, so that if in future they think the interests of the country would be better served by a discussion in camera it would be up to them to make their representations to whom it may concern.
What appeared in Maclean's establishes clearly that	those who	at	that	time saidCanada was	in danger	of	being attackedwere right.	It has taken	some	years toprove those	statements,	but the	facts are
set out in this widely circulated periodical, which quotes the official report.
Even at the time of conscription no one opposed the defence of Canada. The subject matter of the argument was whether it was necessary to defend Canada in Canada, or not. The U-boats coming so far up the St. Lawrence river showed clearly that there was reason for concern.
There was considerable discussion about conscription at the time and Colonel Ralston, who was then minister of defence, resigned because he felt conscription had not been imposed early enough. I should like to know how many men were conscripted for overseas service after the legislation was passed. I had some correspondence with the parliamentary assistant to the minister and he gave me some information, but it is far from complete. I should like the brass hats to work on it and give the committee complete data as to the number of N.R.M.A. men who were conscripted for overseas service after the mobilization act was amended. I received some information, and I translate from a letter in French:
It has been brought to my attention that a publication entitled, "Canada at War" No. 45 of 1945, published by the wartime information services, contains the information you asked for. According to that article 13,000 men were called up by virtue of the mobilization act and were sent overseas to Europe on D-day. Moreover, 3,000 men sailed for overseas after having signed for voluntary service.
I have a clipping to the same effect. I asked three questions, as follows:
1. On what date did the 3,000 men sail for overseas and from what provinces did they come?	i

That is not all the information I wanted, but I thank the parliamentary assistant for what he has sent me. It is now possible to talk sensibly about this matter, but it was not possible during the war. Those who were talking against conscription for overseas were described as isolationists and there was hardly anything that was not said about them. They were told they were not good citizens, they were not patriotic and were not doing their duty. The issue at that time was whether conscription for overseas service was actually helpful to the allied cause at the time the amendment was made. My contention was that it was not.
I crossed the floor of the house with other Liberal members because I was not satisfied with the policy adopted by my party at that time. We were called into a caucus to discuss conscription. The caucus was adjourned, Sir John Dill was here in the east block, the day after Mr. King did not return to the caucus and we were told of the quick turnabout, and conscription for overseas was announced as the policy of the government. I still wonder if it was not just political expediency.
I endeavoured to do my duty in the house by protesting against it in order to protect the farmers and those men who were engaged in essential industry. I was greatly surprised to notice in the Windsor station, the Canadian National station in Montreal, and in other places, that posters were put up stating that the men who were prepared to leave their essential positions to go into the army were doing a better job than if they continued in
Supply-National Defence their present positions. Of course, that was a matter of opinion. If we are believers in fundamental freedoms and human rights contrary opinions must be respected.
I view the future with some alarm because of certain things that are being done. We are likely to be at war with any country and we should look at the facts. Lord Carnarvon, who sponsored the British North America Act and who was unquestionably a great man, stated that the only danger to Canada would come from the United States. That was said at the time of the Fenian raids. That great English statesman felt that Canada was in danger from the United States and in his speech he referred to the number of men between the ages of 16 and 30 who could carry arms for the defence of this country.
I think that all hon. members who were opposed to conscription were opposed because they felt that the defence of Canada was not sufficient at the time. Nobody thought of the defence of Canada, although some of our statesmen and leaders of parties were telling us that Hitler had his eyes on Canada, that Canada would be a prize for him, and that he wanted to get hold of this country. I hope the fears of war expressed by the hon. member who spoke just before me, and by others, are exaggerated. I hope so, but I want to make it clear that nobody is opposed to the defence of Canada, and nobody is opposed to conscription for the defence of Canada, provided that the military authorities do not interfere with essential war services in times of war.
Perhaps what has been said by the leader of the opposition and by my good friend from Nanaimo is right. Perhaps there is some exaggeration in it. I am not in a position to say. If they go anywhere in the province of Quebec and ask the people what their views are about the defence of Canada, they will realize that the concern expressed in the house exists in the province of Quebec just as it does in every other province of Canada from Newfoundland to British Columbia. The people want this country to be defended just as well as it can be, and we rely on the Minister of National Defence to do all he can to further that purpose in the national interest. God forbid that we should have another war, but if we do we hope that Canada will be better defended than it was during the last war.
The answer will be made that the steps taken by Canada during the last war served to protect this country against aggression. There are great changes. When Lord Carnarvon spoke of the danger that might come to Canada from the United States, communications were not the same as they were-

Supply-National Defence during the last war. Since the last war various means of communication have made such progress that every part of the world can be easily exposed to danger, and requires protection. That being said, I should like to congratulate the minister upon the steps he has taken, and I hope that all the criticism that will be made of his department will be constructive. Those who will criticize may be right or wrong, but as long as constructive criticism is offered in good faith I am sure that all those who do so will render a public service.

It would seem that this item forms the basis for a broad discussion of many matters. I am interested in a specific question. I refer to the proposal to build armouries in the city of Saskatoon. I am interested, as are all hon. members, in the welfare of my constituents. The construction of an armoury will provide a good deal of work, and it is a good thing for any city to have such a project being carried on. This proposition is now getting to be somewhat ancient in that responsible ministers of the crown have given their assurance that such construction would take place some time.
I remember it was my pleasant privilege to listen to a fine address -by the present Minister of National Defence at a meeting of the Canadian Club, I believe, in my own city. He assured the members of the club that this project was on the books so far as the government was concerned, and that it was merely a matter of time until construction would be commenced. It was my pleasant duty to move a vote of thanks to the minister for his address. While the hon. member for Calgary East asks a great many questions and makes a great many accusations, neither he nor the minister says anything about what is going to be done to cure the situation. It is for that purpose that I get to my feet.

Supply-National Defence
I think there are several things wrong. In the first place, I do not think the Department of National Defence can be effectively and efficiently run by one minister. There is no one man in this country, I do not care how well qualified he is, who can undertake the responsibility of administering the affairs of the army, the navy and the air force on the scale that we are organizing them today. As long as we have just one minister and one parliamentary assistant, we are going to continue to get the kind of thing that we are getting, as exemplified by what has happened on these estimates. It is rather unfortunate that the minister, the Prime Minister and the members of this committee are obliged to get their information from the Financial Post, or some other newspaper, with regard to a matter that directly affects the security of this country.
I am not blaming the minister for not knowing about this matter because he did not know when this matter was raised. Neither did the Prime Minister. While the minister says that there is no suggestion at all of a leak anywhere in the film board or in any other government department, the fact that Kenneth Wilson had that story before the minister, and that it was published in that newspaper two days ahead of the dateline of that newspaper, proves to me conclusively that there is somebody talking in the film board, the minister's department or somewhere else. Otherwise, where did Kenneth Wilson get this story that he had in the Financial Post?
As members of the House of Commons, I think our first concern is to ascertain whether the minister, with one parliamentary assistant, has an impossible job on his hands in trying to keep track of all of the ramifications of this department. In the second place, the national film board does not come under him directly. It comes under the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I am suggesting that we should determine whether we need more ministers, whether we need that department broken up, or whether we should have sufficient personnel put there to assure us that the responsible minister, coming into this house to answer our questions, has at least time enough to handle the affairs of the department and to know some of the answers, or whether we need maybe another parliamentary assistant for naval affairs and one for the air force who will take some responsibility with regard to answering in the house questions pertaining to the administration of the navy or the air force. I think the minister is in an impossible position in trying to keep track of all these matters.

It was not yesterday that this film board became suspect. We remember the espionage trials. We remember Freda Linton, and the position she occupied on that board. We remember the chairman of the board who is no longer in this country. But the thing I am concerned about with regard to the board is the way the personnel are employed. They do not go through the civil service. I believe the chairman of the board has the right to hire and select all personnel. According to the answer given in the house this morning by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, he is now chairman of the board as well as being the minister responsible for the operations of the board. Because the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is plenty tangled up in housing, I cannot see how he can keep his finger on the technical work that some 500 people are doing, and expect to be informed in the matter.
In my view the board should be brought under the civil service commission. The time to screen government employees is not after they are hired; they should be screened when they are taken in. If the civil service commission were employing members of the film board they would be screened when they were employed. Employees have the right to take part in competitive examinations, at which times they are supposed to give their background; and they are screened on the way in. I think it is an improper procedure to employ 500 people over whose employment the government had no jurisdiction, and then to ask the R.C.M.P. to screen them. These people handled educational films for the Department of National Defence and for other organizations in Canada during the process of fighting a war. In my view the board should be brought within the control of the civil service commission, and they should be screened on the way in. The R.C.M.P. screened them. Who screened the R.C.M.P.? One could go on and on and on with that sort of thing.
My suggestion is that the board should be placed under the civil service commission. It is an imposition to ask the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to accept the responsibility for the operation of the board, and to be responsible to the house for what it does. With all due respect to his capacity, I do not think he can do that kind of job; it would be an impossibility.
It would be unfair to expect the Minister of National Defence to keep his finger on everything pertaining to defence. I have said that no suggestions were made. I shall make two, the first of which is that there should be a check on defence to see if it is not necessary to have someone to assist the minister in

keeping his finger on all the machinery of defence. My second suggestion is that instead of screening employees of the film board after they are employed, they should be screened on the way in. Perhaps the reason we do so much screening lies in the fact that in the whole set-up there are too many patronage appointments. Sometimes the commission appears to me as just a smoke screen behind which people hide in order to make patronage appointments.
Then, with regard to defence matters, and the organization set-up, may I say I believe the minister-or someone for him-has done a good job in the preparation of "Canada's Defence Program", which has been set before us. I am pleased to see that in the report he stresses the fact that it is a defence program. Not only that, but as best he can he tries in this document to dispel references to the inevitability of war. I liked that feature of it.
There can be no defence of this country by ourselves. We would not be able to defend our long coast lines, and our defence program will have to be linked up with those of other countries in the event of this continent or country being invaded. Our link-up with the United States in the North Atlantic pact gives us that assurance. The point upon which I am critical, and which has not been stressed, is that of research. The hon. member for Nanaimo and others have discussed the development of airfields and matters of technical research. I shall not repeat what they have said; but in the breaking down of the defence dollar, instead of giving more of that dollar for research purposes the amount has been cut down by one per cent. This is done in the light of the fact that technical personnel will be expected to fight the next war, and the greatest development will be in the air. The amount allocated last year was six per cent, while this year it is only five per cent. In my view it should be at least ten per cent.
Then at page 25 of the defence program set out by the minister we find something upon which no stress has been placed during this debate:
In the second world war the Canadian forces had one motor vehicle for every four men and one wireless set for every twelve. All three services use equipment like radar, predictors and other complicated electrical and mechanical devices to a degree that is not commonly recognized. Of the officers and other ranks, no less than 74 per cent require special technical qualifications recognized as such in their service.
Greatest bottleneck in meeting a future emergency would not be in raw materials or tools or industrial know-how, still less would it be in trained sailors, soldiers or airmen; it would be in trained tradesmen. Steps are being taken to increase their numbers.
Supply-National Defence
I do not know what steps are being taken in central and western Canada, but I do know none has been taken in the maritime provinces. I leave this thought with the minister-because I think he is absolutely right-that there are approximately 260,000 unemployed in this country, of whom most are young and many are service personnel from the last war. While great stress has been placed upon university education, and while the wonderful job done in that direction has been mentioned frequently in the house- and properly so-let us remember that the minister is correct in his analysis when he states that in another war trained tradesmen will be perhaps more essential than service personnel, as we understand them today.
What this country lacks from coast to coast, and has lacked for a long time, not only in the field of defence but in the whole economy of the country, is a well-developed vocational training program through which people would be trained in the trades. While we may try to be a university country, with everyone a doctor, a musician or a journalist, we will still need the hewers of wood and the drawers of water, the people who create the wealth. We are doing very little to develop those people. If the Department of National Defence could augment what is being done in the field of vocational training by the Department of Labour, and the little the provinces are attempting to do, it would be a good defence investment.
While the minister has stated that steps are being taken to provide permanent service personnel with married quarters, the present situation leaves much to be desired. There are still many service personnel right here in Ottawa and in other centres in Canada where there are concentrations of the permanent force, men with wives and children, who are paying $60 a month rent. They are not living in barracks, and they are placed at a terrific handicap. The program in this respect should be stepped up, because we cannot have happy soldiers or other service personnel unless they are in homes where they may have some comforts and are able to meet the rent.
My chief purpose in speaking was to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that I do not think one man can handle the many tasks which have to be handled by the Minister of National Defence. The hon. member's point has already been met as far as this department is concerned, and I believe that is the case with all other departments.
Then the hon. member doubted if one minister could handle all the ramifications of defence. I must confess that they keep one with a considerable physique busy for a good many hours a day, but I would point out that this instance can hardly be used as an illustration to support his point. I am responsible for the security of the Department of National Defence and we have taken adequate measures to protect that security. We know of no way in which it has been broken with regard to either films or anything else. Then with regard to this particular matter, I was familiar with it from the time I mentioned in May, 1949, and even before that. There has been no failure on my part as far as ensuring security from the defence point of view is concerned.
I am much obliged to the hon. member for his helpful support with regard to married quarters. I can assure him that we are doing everything possible. If he looks at the

in proportion have done more in the way of providing married quarters for our service personnel than, has been done by the other countries with which comparisons are usually made. We regard it as of first importance that we should complete or convert or provide by one means or another as many quarters as we can for married personnel so as to provide them with the amenities of life in a good community. That is our objective.
The hon. member made a very good suggestion with regard to the training of tradesmen, a suggestion which is directly in line with what we are doing. Supplementing the vocational work carried on by the provinces and the federal government working in co-operation, last year we started an interesting experiment. We took 200 boys out of the vocational schools of Ontario and gave them special training at Ipperwash camp for six weeks. This was in addition to the ordinary cadet work. They received training in wireless, motor vehicle maintenance and similar branches of the technical services related to the armed forces. If they satisfied the requirements after their six weeks' training they were given a bonus of $60.
We invited representatives of all the provincial governments to attend this experiment and I am glad to say that they all sent representatives. Several provinces sent their deputy ministers of labour. Naturally I cannot speak for the provincial governments but I think I can say that the reactions of those who attended the demonstrations were favourable. We extended the plan this year to include 1,100 cadets to be trained at a number of different camps, and here again we secured the wholehearted support of the vocational schools. Eleven hundred is a considerable number of boys to interest in this work, and we hope it is just a beginning.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to direct the attention of the minister to paragraph 156 on page 35 of the excellent booklet he has put out. It is stated there that the Newfoundland regiment and the 166th artillery regiment have been authorized to perpetuate their fine records in the first and second world wars. A daily newspaper of St. John's on Thursday, November 17, reports a communique issued by the commanding officer stating that three regiments have been authorized and recruiting is taking place. It is stated that those regiments are to be stationed at St. John's, Grand Falls and Corner Brook, but apparently no provision is being made for a unit at Gander and Goose airports. I know very little of defence matters but in my humble opinion a unit of some nature should be stationed at Gander at all times. Possibly we could have an explanation from the minister.
This article gives the strength of the Newfoundland regiment as 380 officers and noncommissioned officers and 632 other ranks. That would appear to be a high proportion of officers. I do not know whether it is correct. The strengths of the other regiments are out of line. The Newfoundland field regiment has 380 officers and 632 men; the 59th independent field squadron, Royal Canadian Engineers, has ten officers and 299 other ranks, and the Newfoundland regiment has 38 officers and 812 other ranks. I presume it is intended to increase the personnel of these units later on.
I feel, in so far as Gander and Goose are concerned, some definite steps should be taken to provide a defence unit at both these places. The stationing of a unit at Corner Brook is hardly necessary, in my opinion, because the United States army based at Harmon field is very close. Even at St. John's there is a large
Supply-National Defence United States base, but there is nothing whatsoever at Gander. I think there is a United States unit at Goose, but I do not know whether or not there is a Canadian unit.
I should like to refer to the position of the naval establishment. During the past war Canada had a large number of naval bases-
I suppose we can put it that way-around Newfoundland and Labrador, and also a number of radio stations forming a radio hook-up. To my knowledge a number of these have been discontinued, and an attempt is being made to sell them. I believe some have been dismantled, but it seems to me to be a great waste of money. If they have to be repurchased or other properties bought it will mean a great waste of money. At the naval base at Bay Bulls there was a very fine dry dock. They used to pull corvettes out there when they came for repairs. I believe that has been sold, although word has come to me quite recently that the navy intends to buy it back again. I do not know whether or not that is the position. I think we should have some clarification.
Then I should like to refer to the port facilities at St. John's. I should like to know what the intention is. In the same paragraph it is stated:
We have also commenced negotiations to acquire the admiralty properties in St. John's.
Does that mean all of the properties owned by the Royal Navy? How far have negotiations gone? Are the properties to be purchased, or is it a matter of care and maintenance? What is the position? They are quite extensive, and I know they cost a lot of money at the time they were put in service.
I wish to discuss two further matters, and then I shall have finished. In paragraph 157 on page 35 it says:
Negotiations have been entered upon to secure modification of certain of the U.S. rights at the bases leased by the United Kingdom.
I do not know whether the minister can tell us at the present time how far these discussions have proceeded. Can he tell us what modification is being sought? I am sure he is aware of the article in Maclean's magazine recently written by Mr. Blair Fraser. I would say the contents of the article are pretty critically correct, as we say in Newfoundland. There may be some slight divergences, but I would say it is critically correct. I should like to know about these modifications, and whether they have to do with the troubles we are having, as set forth in that article.
The last matter to which I should like to direct attention is this, and I am not sure whether it is proper to raise it at this time. I have been told since coming to Ottawa that

Supply-National Defence communist schools are being openly operated, that they are taking children and indoctrinating them with communist ideas. I believe these schools are well known to the mounted police and to the minister. It seems to me to be a most peculiar situation to have this kind of cancer growth in the country openly eating at the vitals of our whole defence system. No matter what we may feel about freedom of thought and speech, it does not seem to me to be sensible to allow schools of that nature to carry on in Canada today.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member about the strengths of the units, these strengths are what they are authorized to recruit at the present time. There were no reserve forces in Newfoundland either between the first and second world wars or since the second world war, and since these units are just being organized the strengths naturally are heavy in officer and N.C.O. personnel. These will be needed to recruit and train the rest.
As to the protection of Gander and Goose, as I stated to the hon. member for Nanaimo last week, at Goose there is a considerable force of United States and Canadian air force personnel and servicing units. At Gander there is only a small handful of Canadian personnel.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Only seven.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right. It is not part of our immediate plan to put active force personnel especially to guard all air establishments across Canada. If we were to distribute our active force personnel in static defence across Canada we would not be getting on with the other jobs which we think have a higher priority. If an emergency seems likely to arise, or should it arise, then it would be possible to take effective measures promptly to defend such places. As to the location of the reserve force units, the hon. member expressed surprise that one should be located at Corner Brook. Corner Brook is the second largest community in Newfoundland. Its population took a very active part in both the navy and the army in the first and second world wars, and contributed a great number of men.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: It is not for defence purposes?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Not for full-time defence. It is for the purpose of organizing reserve units which would be available for use anywhere they were needed, but which incidentally would be immediately available for the defence of Corner Brook or any other part of Newfoundland. That would be their primary purpose. When I was in Corner Brook in July 1 had the pleasure of meeting representatives of the city, of the Legion,

and of the local company, Bowater's Limited. They expressed great interest in the formation of reserve units and promised active support. We thought it desirable to locate units at St. John's, Grand Falls and Corner Brook. We have very good accommodation for the reserve navy and army at St. John's, and we are moving hangars from another location to be used for army and navy training at Grand Falls and Corner Brook.
As to the naval bases, we are still negotiating with representatives of the admiralty. We are not going to acquire all twenty-two properties in St. John's because some of them have already been disposed of to the government of Newfoundland. We are going to take over a majority of them. We are only going to use now those which are useful in peacetime, but we hope to develop later one or two so that they can be put into immediate use in the event of war.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Before you go on, may I ask if any of these units are to become permanent active units?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No, not at the present time. In connection with the operation of the naval reserve division at St. John's, and we hope later at Corner Brook, there would be about thirty active navy personnel, petty officers and men, to assist in training, looking after equipment and the like. At a later stage we hope to have the means of developing one or two permanent defence establishments, in connection with the defence of Newfoundland. The hon. member referred to the base at Bay Bulls. I also saw that base, and having seen it I must say that it was big, indeed an amazing job. But I think the advice followed by the authorities at the time was sound; that is, that it would be a good thing to let some private individual have it and carry it on, and such part as could be usefully employed again in the event of an emergency would still be there to be taken over if necessary, but that it would not be desirable to operate that great establishment in peacetime.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But it has been sold outright.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but it cannot be taken away; it is too big for that. Such part as might still be useful to help meet any emergency which could arise in the near future could still be taken over.
With respect to negotiations with the United States government for modification of the lease agreements, the modifications we seek are those related to what may be called the non-military rights conferred by the leases, rights of extraterritoriality similar to those conferred by the British government under the stress of the crisis of 1941 at places other than Newfoundland. We believe the rights

enjoyed by the United States military authorities in Newfoundland should be the same as we give them under the operation of Cana

dian laws in other parts of Canada. As hon. members know, these rights are reciprocal. United States forces in Canada have the same rights in every respect as Canadian forces enjoy in the United States. We believe the principle of the declaration of February 12, 1947, should be applied to the Newfoundland bases and our representations have gone forward to that effect.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: How far have they gone now?

speechtext: Then just one final question; would there be any comment at all on the matter of communist schools?

speechtext: That matter should be referred to the Minister of Justice. In referring to this matter the hon. gentleman said "as the minister well knows." I do not know of the existence of such schools in Canada, but that may be because I am too innocent.

I have just one short question to direct to the minister, arising out of a question I placed on the order paper the other day. It was answered by the Department of National Defence on October 31, and had to do with flying risk allowance. I shall just read the pertinent parts of the question and the answers given by the department:
4.	Under what conditions is risk allowance given?
5.	What is the amount payable?
The answers were:
4.	Risk allowance is payable to:
(a)	Aircrew officers on, the strength of units whose normal function is flying.
(b)	Aircrew officers not on the strength of flying units, provided they fly as members of an aircrew for not less than eight hours per month.
(c)	Personnel undergoing flying training, for the full period of such training.
Then this is the answer in which I am more interested:
(d)	Other ranks who form part of the crews of aircraft in accordance with established quotas, ranging from one crewman for every four two-seater aircraft to four crewmen for each multiengined aircraft engaged in photographic operations and fitted with Shoran equipment.
5.	$30 per month for all ranks.
It has been brought to my attention since I have been in Ottawa, and when I was in 45781-140
Supply-National Defence Calgary, that aircrew mechanics are compelled in the ordinary discharge of their duties to fly aircraft, but when they do so they do not receive the risk allowance. That was what led me to put the question on the order paper. I should like the minister to tell us whether it is definitely true that these men who in the course of their ordinary duties are required to fly, whether they be aircraft mechanics or others, are being paid that flying risk allowance. I am definitely assured that they are not.
The minister may say, as in fact I pointed out to those who drew this matter to my attention, that the proper thing would be for these people to go to their commanding officers. After having been in this house for so long, however, I know, as the minister knows, that this sort of thing is not done in the air force. Personnel do not go to the commanding officer on such questions. It just is not considered etiquette, and reprisals might be suffered by these men if they were to go to their commanding officers on such a matter. I am told on good authority, however, that there are aircrew who in the ordinary course of their duties are compelled to fly aircraft but are not in receipt of this flying risk allowance the government says is being paid.

speechtext: I am sure the hon. member has in mind the case of air mechanics who are servicing aircraft on the ground and in the course of testing them go up with the aircraft for a limited period of time and do not get the risk allowance during that period.

Supply-National Defence

speechtext: Saint John has a dockyard, too.

speechtext:
I remember that during the war less than two per cent of the expenditures for war supplies went to the maritimes. This is quite in contrast with the statement made by the hon. member for Westmorland, whom I would congratulate on his remarks. He is very proud of his unit, the Princess Louise Hussars, and with very good reason. I might remark in passing that the headquarters of the Princess Louise Hussars is in my home town of Sussex, and we are also very proud of this unit. According to the hon. member, and I think also the minister, recruiting in the maritime provinces has been and is better than in any other part of Canada, and that being so I think we should receive greater recognition in matters pertaining to the manufacture and sale of military equipment.
I was amazed to hear the hon. member compare recruiting now with recruiting before the last war. I remember being in this house before the second war when this department asked parliament for between $30 million and $40 million. At that time many hon. members were opposed to voting that money, and I remember that one hon. member was even willing to reduce the amount to $1. In contrast with that, Mr. Chairman, before the war we find we were trying to carry on with estimates of between $30 million and $40 million, while today we have estimates of $350 million. There is no comparison at all. When the minister said there were as many men in the reserve forces in those days as there are today- well, to me it is quite amazing. We should have many, many more, not only because of the large amount of money that is being expended but because of the better accommodation for the troops and the sentiment in this country which is more favourable towards recruiting than it was in those days.
I believe the minister is quite fortunate, Mr. Chairman, in that he has behind him in Canada today almost a unanimous sentiment so far as military estimates are concerned, something which has never existed in this country before. There is no particular reason for it, but I rather surmise it is due to the fact there is not the same sense of security today as prevailed in this country previous to the last war. My seatmate, the member for Broadview (Mr. Church), has expressed the view on numerous occasions that we were secure because Great Britain had control of the sea. For a hundred years Great Britain was our chief barrier of 
defence. Today, she is not. For that reason, I believe Canadians today are more defence * conscious than they have ever been before.
My principal reason for speaking, Mr. Chairman, was to suggest to the minister that in the training of artillery, for instance, it would be better to have the artillery from the maritime provinces trained in the maritime provinces, instead of sending them to Petawawa. There is a camp at Tracadie, New Brunswick, which was used during the war and I believe it is still possible to train there. I feel that much better results would be obtained if that camp were used instead of wasting time bringing the men up to Petawawa. I say "wasting time" because last summer I believe the men had two weeks for camp. Two days are consumed in the journey to Petawawa, one day is always used after the men arrive in preparing for training the next day, and then in breaking camp another day is lost plus the two days for the return journey, making a total of six days, which is just wasted time. I suggest to the minister that far more men in these units would go into camp, and valuable time would be saved, if my proposal were adopted.
I had prepared a number of matters to bring to the attention of the house, Mr. Chairman, but I do not intend to speak on them this afternoon. The other day I was a little disappointed when the minister spoke of civilian defence. He suggested that civilian defence could be left in abeyance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No, sir, I did not; the local organizations at the block level could be postponed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not agree with the minister. I believe it is necessary to have local defence committees set up. In time of trouble, I do not believe these people can be trained. The minister said that they would be "browned off", or words to that effect. It seems to me that once they get their training, even though they do become lax or careless, that is something they carry with them and there is an organization available to be called upon.
I was reading an article about defence in Sweden. I have it before me, but I am not going to read it. In that country, they lay particular emphasis on this fact, and have the population in the large centres well trained. I believe we could follow their example.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
In answer to the question about training artillery in the maritime provinces, that is receiving consideration. I looked into it myself when it was brought to my attention, and the objections to it are that it would require additional staff,

for administration, training and housekeeping, and a splitting up of equipment. It would also prevent the artillery training in Tracadie from having the advantages of association with other arms which they have now in Petawawa where armoured and other units are in training. As hon. members know, every week during the training season there is a striking demonstration of fire power and modern tactics there. The matter is receiving consideration, however.
With regard to civilian defence I did not say we were not going to do anything, even in the matter of local organization. We are moving up step by step from federal, provincial, municipal and then to local organizations. We believe that is the right way to do it. We have not felt it desirable to rush in to the local field. We are going to press forward with that as soon as we can build the desired organization and get the full support of the local authorities.

speechtext: When I rose the other evening to make an appeal on behalf of the reserve officers, instructors and cadet corps to have their pay exempt from income tax, the minister said that a provision in the Income Tax Act was holding it up, and a formula was needed whereby the pay of those men would not be considered as income. Supply-National Defence seen it stated that the minister is going to Europe within a short time to attend a conference at Paris. speechtext:
At Paris, on November 29, there will be a meeting of the military committee under the North Atlantic treaty; that is a committee of the chiefs of staffs of the twelve powers. Canada will be represented at that by Lieutenant General Charles Foulkes, chief of the Canadian general staff and chairman of the chiefs of staff committee. Since we want to save on transportation costs,
I shall go in the plane with him. We shall be accompanied by Air Vice Marshal Hugh Campbell, our senior liaison officer in the north Atlantic security organization and our principal staff officer at Washington, and also by a representative of the navy, Commodore Bidwell. We shall be joined in Paris by Lieutenant General Clark, who is our representative in England, the chairman of the joint staff there, and who is our observer in connection with the western European group under the North Atlantic treaty.
At Paris there will also be a meeting of the defence committee consisting of the defence ministers, which has been called by the secretary of defence of the United States, Louis Johnson who is chairman of the committee. The committee will discuss arrangements in connection with the organization of the north Atlantic regional groups and other matters relating to its work. The proceedings of the defence committee, like those of the military committee, have so far been regarded as secret. I imagine that the proceedings of these meetings will also be regarded as secret and therefore it would be quite improper for me to anticipate what would be discussed there as I think it may prove impossible for me to report on what happens there except in accordance with an agreed statement. However, this marks a further stage in the organization of north Atlantic security under the treaty, and that organization is proceeding rapidly and satisfactorily.

When the house rose on Friday I had been asking the minister a few questions in connection with the specific items as they appear in the details of services. At that time we were discussing the ones headed "Personnel supplies and services". subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The next item as to which I have a note has to do with the photographic squadron. I see that the estimate for it is up from approximately $868,000 to $1,967,605. Personally I think the photographic squadron can be extremely useful to Canada not only for the defence forces but for other departments of the government. As a matter of fact, I see there is a repayment of $940,000 to the department from the Department of Mines and Resources. I should like to ask the minister how much of the work done by the photographic squadron is performed for other departments and how much is done for military mapping.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is a very interesting question. We have been conducting a photographic survey of Canada supplementing and completing that already undertaken and carried through by the R.C.A.F. during the lean years from 1924 on. This has been one of the ways in which the R.C.A.F. kept alive during the period between wars. Last year our program was to complete about 800,000
Supply-National Defence miles of photography, and we exceeded that. This year a corresponding area has been covered, and that is probably the greatest amount of serial photography ever conducted. It is done by the R.C.A.F. using twenty-two planes operating in all sorts of weather.
The results are taken to the photographic establishment at Rockcliffe where they process some 100,000 films per month. Then these are put together in a mosiac and then turned over to the Department of Mines and Resources, which department performs the fundamental work of producing a basic map. That map is developed for various purposes, topographical, mineralogical and military. The map is used as a basis for civil and military purposes, and is used not only by a great number of our government departments but also by provincial government departments, and by the three services. It is a fine demonstration of the way in which government departments work together. This is done by the R.C.A.F. working in the air, by Royal Canadian Engineers working on base marks, and by the Department of Mines and Resources working through their own topographical experts. This is a field in which I venture to say that, through the combination of these elements, Canada takes second place to no country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I agree with the minister that this particular branch of the R.C.A.F. is an important and useful one. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I think that is a very much better way of accounting, and I am glad to hear that it has been done. My next question is in regard to the northwest staging route. The total cost of this is up approximately $1,300,000, but I notice that the fuel costs are down from $630,000 to $291,000.
