subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: There was an over-provision last year which has been rectified this year.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I have only one more question.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Hurrah!

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The cheering which greets that announcement indicates that those who made the noise have no interest whatever in these estimates, but are only interested in getting away from here as soon as possible so they can go home for Christmas. My question has to do with the general position in connection with commitments. At the end of the details I see this note:
Less-Estimated amount required for commitments nominally to fall due during the fiscal year, in accordance with navy, army and air force programs detailed above, but not required for actual expenditure in that year, $62,500,000.
Then in the general estimates under item 250 we have "commitments for future years of $145,555,382". I should like to know why it is necessary to have two commitments for future years, which is what this amounts to. The department is asking for commitments of $62,500,000 in this year's estimates to be spent next year or some subsequent year; then further authorization is asked for commitments of $145,500,000, also to be spent in subsequent years. Why does it appear in that form; why cannot one item suffice?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The answer is given in paragraph 53 of the white paper, which I shall read because probably it is briefer than I might be:
Experience has shown that orders for equipment and other services for the armed forces often cannot be completed in the same year in which the

contracts are placed. At the same time it is not possible to say just which of such contracts will be completed in the fiscal year. Authority is therefore requested in the estimates put forward by the department to provide for the anticipated program, but at the same time to limit the appropriation to the cash expenditures which it is expected will be made against these contracts. Future years commitment authority is requested to cover contracts for equipment and services which it is known will not be received in whole or in part until after the current fiscal year.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But why is the second item necessary? Surely there can be no question but that if the house is not prepared to vote these further amounts two years or three years from now, or whenever they may be required, they will not be available in any event. In other words the house is always able to vote or withhold money. If the house should be unwilling to vote it the money would not be available, so why provide for it two or three years ahead of time? I still cannot see why the one item covering what might be spent but is not immediately in view for the coming year should not be enough.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I sympathize with the hon. gentleman, but the point is that in order to produce modern naval, military and air equipment a contract must be entered into which may not be completed during the current fiscal year. Take ships. We have entered into contracts this year for the construction of one icebreaker, three anti-submarine vessels, four minesweepers and one gate vessel, the total cost of which will be between forty and forty-five million dollars. It is quite certain that none of these vessels will be completed in the fiscal year 1949-50. It is also quite certain that almost none will be completed in the fiscal year 1950-51. Yet in order to enter into a contract which the contractors will regard as at least morally binding and as having the authority given by parliament through these commitments, we must be able to do so on the assumption that any parliament subsequently elected will honour those authorizations and commitments. Otherwise we could not make a contract running into the future. This is one of the ways by which we may provide a defence program over a term of years, which parliament will know about in advance and provide commitment authority for in advance, but in respect of which parliament must provide the cash year by year.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Would the minister not agree that a contract would be quite as good whether or not this advance commitment is made, because it depends on the particular year when the estimates are voted, whether or not parliament is willing to grant the money? I cannot see any advantage in it.

The minister said people entering into these contracts consider that these commitments give them greater moral value, let us say; but X should think once Canada has entered into a contract for the construction of a destroyer, an icebreaker, an anti-aircraft gun, or whatever it may be, we are going to honour that commitment. It is not necessary for us to vote money two or three years ahead more or less tentatively, in order to do that. My chief objection is that it complicates the estimates, so it is very difficult to tell exactly where we stand. We vote so much money for current requirements and so much for what may be required because the department could not foresee what would happen; then we have another long series of commitments for two or three years from now.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The fact is that parliament cannot provide the cash to meet these possible expenditures in future years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is my very point.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But parliament can say that we commit the authority of the government for a future year. That will have some value to the contractor, and I can assure my hon. friend that it also acts as a limiting factor on the department.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The point is that parliament actually cannot commit itself to these expenditures for next year, as the minister just said. We have no power to do that; the money has to be voted each year. That is why I cannot see any value in putting in these items, because they confuse the issue.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not going to ask very many questions after the barrage that the minister has been up against in the last half hour. I should like to make a short observation. When the estimates were before the committee a week ago, I asked the minister a question about the armouries for Charlottetown and also a naval base. At that time he gave me fair consideration and stated that those would be built in the near future. The total estimates before us for this department amount to $369,985,500, and they are the only estimates out of the whole of the main estimates that have been brought down for which the minister does not ask for a blank cheque to be voted without giving any details. If the minister is willing to take a compliment from a humble member of the back benches, may I say that in this regard his estimates are much superior to the estimates presented for any other department.
It is true that in the estimates for this department there is an item for sundries amounting to $4,695,252, but if one looks
Supply-National Defence at the pages upon which details are given one finds details for all those amounts. The other ministers of the crown bring in estimates containing items amounting to $131 million for which they ask us to give them a blank cheque. I should like to compliment this minister and his department for bringing down estimates for which we do not have to give a blank cheque.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask a question about the imperial war graves commission. I do not believe anyone would question the amount of money spent, but is this for the maintenance of world war I graves or world war II graves or both? In what countries in Europe does this commission work?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
This item looks after our contribution to the imperial war graves commission in respect of the great war of 1914-1918 as well as the second world war. The war graves provided for in the second world war are in Italy, France, Belgium, Holland and England. The arrangement under which it is worked out is between the countries of the commonwealth. It was worked out towards the end of the first world war and has been carried on ever since. We have agreed on a common treatment of the subject, so as to afford the maximum amount of respect and reverence for the graves of those who were killed from all the commonwealth countries. We agreed that the treatment should be the same, not only in respect of officers and men but also of those who gave their lives in the service of all the commonwealth countries.
Then, we agreed on a method of administration and of contribution. We have carried through our part in that arrangement. We believe it has worked well in the interests of the memory of those who gave their lives.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What about the graves of the men who fell in Asia?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I beg your pardon, they are also being looked after under the same arrangement.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Last fall, I came back on the boat with a chap who was a citizen of Ottawa. He had been looking for the grave of his son. I do not remember the name of the cemetery, but he had been there twice and was not able to find a single person who could give him directions. He told me that at the time there was a stick with his son's name on it, which they finally discovered. That was the second trip they had made to England to find their son's grave, and they found it in the same condition as it was the year before. If necessary, I can give the minister the name privately.

Supply-National Defence

speechtext: I would be very glad if the hon. member did that because that case has certainly not been called to my attention. In the first world war we had some 66,000 killed and in this war 40,000. If the hon. gentleman will give me that name, I shall certainly be concerned in following up the case.

speechtext: I am writing the name now. This was in one of the largest cemeteries in England.

speechtext: In England?

Mr. Chairman, the discussion that has taken place and the obvious impatience of some of the members to dispose of these estimates in itself indicates how desirable it would have been if an orderly procedure before a committee could have been followed. This is only the third time these estimates have been before the house. They were up on November 11, November 18, and now today. Members of this house do not know today what the state of our defence forces is; they do not know their readiness or otherwise to fulfil the part which the Minister of National Defence says Canada has decided it should play in the joint responsibilities that we have assumed.
Hon. members of this house have been given the details as to the cost of certain items. They have been given percentages of training which, in themselves, mean very little unless we examine the details of the units that are involved; the standard and quantity of equipment now in the possession of those units; and the extent of the training in the various weapons they possess. The procedure before a committee makes the process of question and answer much more effective than it can be in this chamber, although I want to say that the minister has indicated his readiness to answer the questions which have been asked.
By the procedure which we are now following, we could not obtain the real facts about the national defence forces of this country in three weeks, let alone three sittings of this house. Three months would probably be the amount of time needed under the procedure which we must follow according to the rules of the house. For that reason, I propose to ask certain questions which indicate the nature of the information which it seems to me we must have if we are to have any idea whatever of the real state of the defence forces of this country.
[Air. Smith (Calgary West).]
It does not help greatly to know that an anti-aircraft gun with its equipment costs $600,000, unless you know how many antiaircraft guns we have; unless you know what their radar equipment is; their range finding equipment; their directional equipment; their sound range devices; and all the control equipment that goes with a modern aircraft battery, and the training of the men on each one of those instruments that is associated with an anti-aircraft gun.
Unless I am mistaken, I heard a remark in regard to Russia; and I assume that it meant that Russia would like to have this information. The time has come, Mr. Chairman, when we should recognize that the only people we are fooling are the people of Canada if we do not get all the facts with regard to our national defence. Our capacity to assume whatever role we undertake to assume within that great international partnership created by the North Atlantic security pact depends upon the equipment, the training and the suitability of the various units that we have established, having regard to the conditions which we face today.
The Minister of National Defence within a day or so leaves for Paris to take part in discussions there which will, we hope, divide the field of responsibility in a way that will make it possible to economize-and I underline the word economize-in expenditures on national defence so that every dollar spent may produce the maximum results. It is no more possible for the members of this committee to pass real judgment on the extremely large figure which is now before us, without knowing certain of these details, than it would be for the Calgary Stampeders to know whether their season had been well spent until they knew that they had certain players who were going to take their place in the line on Saturday, whether some of the members see the game or not.
After all, it is only an expansion of the same idea. A military organization is a team. In fact, in the United States during the war there came into use a term which seems remarkably appropriate for the whole defence picture. The forces had what they called "combat teams". These are defence teams. Our job is to know whether we have players for every position on that team, whether he has had the training he should have and whether he has the equipment which will carry him through the game.
First of all, let us take the land forces. Statements have been made as to the proportion of our population that is taking its share in the defence forces of Canada. When certain questions were asked, the answer given was that our reserve units had a total enlistment

which, in relation to our population, constitutes a higher percentage of the population as a whole in the non-active units than any other nation of the commonwealth. That statement, Mr. Chairman, is absolutely meaningless and it is misleading unless one examines what the situation is in other nations of the commonwealth. Let us take, for instance, the situation in the United Kingdom. Apart from what the views of any hon. member may be in regard to one method of dealing with defence requirements or otherwise, the fact is that the United Kingdom has compulsory military service. Consequently you must examine, in the light of that fact, any figures of proportion of the population taking part in defence; and also you must examine the figures in the light of the responsibilities that are being assumed by the active units in the United Kingdom.
Today the United Kingdom has six and a half divisions fully equipped, ready for service outside the United Kingdom in different parts of the world right from Burma to Hong Kong. She has other units in being, fully equipped. There is a provision that every man or woman having served with the active forces must, on retirement from the active forces, serve for four years with the territorials. These are things that it is essential to know in making any comparison or when we are deciding on what the allocation of our forces should be, and whether we should emphasize one branch of the service or the other.
One of the most important statements that have been made since these estimates were called on November 11, if not the most important one, was the statement by the hon. member for Nanaimo that there should be a drastic reorganization of our defence forces in Canada. He stated then that, while he was not presuming to adopt a precise figure, his estimate of the appropriate relationship between the air force and the land army was three to one. The Minister of National Defence obviously misunderstood what he had said, because he took that statement up and said that if you took the figure that is being expended on the land forces today, and multiplied that by three, you would reach a figure that would be out of the question.
The speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo was perfectly clear on that point. What he said was that there must be a drastic operation, a reorganization, a change in the composition of the units, and that there must be an emphasis on the air force in relation to the infantry, having regard to our possible position in the combined defence organization upon which the peace of the world rests In the years ahead.
Supply-National Defence
Without reducing any of this discussion to personalities, may I emphasize the fact that we are particularly fortunate in having in the membership of this committee some men who are in a position to speak to us with regard to national defence matters. When the agriculture estimates were before us, there were in every part of the committee highly .. qualified farmers who were able to ask the Minister of Agriculture various questions based upon their own highly skilled experience in that field. When matters relating to public health are before the house, we have in different parts of the house men whose own medical experience gives them special qualifications. Now that we are dealing with national defence estimates, we are in the position of having men here who are able to speak with a high degree of qualification. There is no other man in this committee with the background of experience of the hon. member for Nanaimo. There is no other member of this committee whose personal service has covered so wide a range of military experience. I do not want to make any comparisons but, after all, let us examine the background of this infantry officer, this permanent force soldier, who tells us that there should be a drastic reorganization and a reduction in the emphasis on infantry and an increase in the emphasis on the air force.
Here in this chamber are two men entitled to wear the highest decoration for valour in the world, the Victoria Cross. These are the hon. member for Nanaimo and the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

I spoke of this chamber-and I think the hon. member will realize that I spoke of this chamber, and no matter how distinguished the service of anyone outside this chamber may be, unfortunately it does not entitle him to come here and speak on military matters.
We have here two members who have that qualification, which is something in itself. But I do wish to point out that the hon. member for Nanaimo, who began as a private in the infantry and who retired with the rank of major-general after having served in two world wars, has been decorated with the Victoria Cross, is a Commander of the Bath, and was awarded the Distinguished Service Order, the Military Cross and the Order of Merit of the United States. There is no other living infantry officer in the world today who is entitled to wear on his breast all those decorations for valour.

Supply-National Defence
I mention that because he comes to us as a member of the House of Commons with that combined experience and tells us, as an infantry officer with many years' experience, that the time has come for Canada to recognize the fact that the role which we must play is one which calls for emphasis upon the air service of this country. That does not mean for one moment that there is any need to lose all the great traditions associated with the different units throughout the country.
I would remind hon. members that drastic operations of a similar nature did take place in the years before the two world wars. The services were carrying forward very much as they ended the war in 1918; and then with a new emphasis on armoured units and larger quantities of artillery and the extension of the engineering services, and of the various technical services, units with long and great traditions in the infantry were changed to the new branches of the service. They retained their names and their association, and have carried that tradition forward through the years since then. The same can be done today.
Many infantry units in different parts of Canada can become reserve air units and carry out various services, not only as squadrons fitted with aircraft, but to carry out the many involved and indirect duties associated with the maintenance of any air force under modem conditions. I refer to radar units, communications units and the other services required to maintain an air force. This can be done.
What is essential is that in examining these enormous expenditures-and they are enormous expenditures-we make sure that there is an allocation of our forces in such a way that we gain the greatest possible value from the money being spent.
For that reason I would like to ask a question, which is the basis of any understanding of our problem in the field of our land forces. I would ask the Minister of National Defence: first of all, in the case of the army, what are the arms of that service today?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers I have a word to say. I appreciate what the leader of the opposition has said about the hon. member for Nanaimo, and I have as much admiration for him as has his leader. I remember that during the session before last, when the deskmate of the hon. member was a Canadian-born member of parliament, I said of the hon. member that although he was not born in this country he was more of a Canadian than was his deskmate.
This is to depreciate no one, but only to give an opportunity to the leader of the opposition to understand that there are things about which we agree with him. We agree about the defence of Canada. But as every country will be exposed during the next war, if there is one-and everyone hopes there will not-I submit it is impossible for the Minister of National Defence to answer publicly any technical questions put to him by any member of the house. If the information can be given privately for the satisfaction of any hon. member, it is an altogether different matter.
Sitting here as the elected representatives of the Canadian people, we have a duty to perform, and must act to the best of our ability to represent our constituents. They must have confidence in us. They must understand that in these difficult matters members of parliament must be given a certain latitude. There are things they can tell privately but could not tell publicly and which if printed in the press would not serve the best interests of the country.
Let me give this illustration to the hon. member: If he were a banker would he publish in any newspaper the combination of his vault or safe? He is too much of a businessman to do anything like that. When it comes to matters of life and death, as applied to every citizen of this country and of the world, one must be very cautious about what is said.
I shall not embark upon any technicalities at this time, but I would remind the hon. member and my colleagues that during the war, although I have no military training and do not pose as a man with military experience -and never did-I suggested that the best possible defence for this country would be mobile units which could be brought as quickly as possible from any part of the country to repel any attack, and to defeat the enemy.
This is a simple thing and something which can be said in public, because any possible enemy would think twice before attacking a country defended by mobile units. That is one thing.
There is another thing that concerns me about which I should like to express my feelings. During the last war a large number of parliamentarians considered matters of defence in the light of the defence of the commonwealth as a whole. Since that time this country has signed the North Atlantic pact and a new solidarity exists, not only between the various parts of the commonwealth but between all the countries that

signed that pact. It is of the utmost importance that we should know the obligations of Canada under that pact. Again this is something that perhaps should not be mentioned in public, but I think any hon. member who desires information about the commitments of Canada under that pact should have it.
I support the minister and I have confidence in him. If there is a vote on this estimate I shall show my confidence by voting for him. But there should be reciprocity in confidence and I say to him that I am concerned about the commitments of Canada under that multilateral pact.
As I said the other day, and as I suggested many years ago, we should have a bilateral treaty of defence with the United States. At that time the then prime minister, who was also secretary of state for external affairs, said that that was not the time for such an agreement. An agreement was made between himself and the President of the United States, but it was never ratified' by congress.
When this country must share matters of defence with other countries I submit that we should retain our sovereignty with regard to the number of people from Canada who will serve for the defence of this or other countries. Many hon. gentlemen have referred to the defence of Canada but they have said nothing about the defence of those other countries which signed the pact.
Canada played a noble part in the last war in supporting the countries of the commonwealth and other countries of the world, but it is important to know what will be done in the future in connection with the defence of the countries who are signatories to the North Atlantic pact. How many men will we send? How much ammunition? What armaments? That information is essential.
I am not ashamed of being a supporter of the government and I am not afraid to speak freely in the House of Commons about these matters of vital importance. If we are to go to the defence of any other country we should have something in return. Canada is just reaching complete sovereignty and her great privilege is to retain that sovereignty in her relations with other countries of the world. We should retain our sovereignty and our independence and should decide ourselves what we are to do. The defence of Canada should not be decided by any other country, either by our friendly neighbour or by the United Kingdom or by the United Kingdom military experts. It should be decided right here by the members of the House of Commons and the Senate.
Supply-National Defence
The leader of the opposition has legal experience. He knows that when a case comes up in court having to do with a scientific or technical matter it is not expected that the judge shall have taken a course in technology or the particular science under review in order to be qualified to decide the case. He decides the case according to his legal experience, the law of the land and his own good judgment. He must be convinced that one of the parties is right in order to give judgment.
This is a somewhat similar case. There are military experts on the other side of the house and on this side of the house. I have the greatest respect for the hon. member for Nanaimo, but I have equal respect for the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of National Defence. Though the Minister of National Defence fought through the war as an N.C.O., no shame should attach to him for that.
The first minister of national defence in the last world war was not even an N.C.O. in the previous war, he was just a private. He was wounded and disabled and was entitled to a pension. He was greatly respected by all. I want the committee to understand that I respect those hon. members who have been mentioned by the leader of the opposition just as much as he respects them, but he should not make a comparison between one of his supporters, who was an officer, and the Minister of National Defence, who was an N.C.O.
Without saying anything against the admirable record of the hon. member for Nanaimo I am not ashamed to say that I support the Minister of National Defence, who was an N.C.O. during the first world war, and I have confidence in him. There should not be conflict between those who have had military service and those who have not. We all have the duty of looking after the interests of the Canadian people as a whole. We should be ready to lay aside those prejudices that existed during the first and second world wars. I rejoiced to hear the hon. member for Nanaimo speak as a true Canadian when he spoke the other day. I congratulate him on what he has said, but he has too much experience to contend that he is infallible. Nobody in this world is infallible. We must make the best approach we can to this matter of common national concern. I will ask the leader of the opposition-and I do so on my own responsibility-whether, all things being said, he would be satisfied to have certain private information conveyed to him in a private way to satisfy his mind so that he will be in a position to tell the Canadian people

Supply-National Defence that he has all the information and is satisfied with it. Then there will be an end to a lengthy discussion. Perhaps, considering the subject matter, it has not been so long.
I want every one of my colleagues to have his mind satisfied as to problems of national importance, and I have enough confidence in them to say publicly that, supported as they are by the votes of their electors in each of the constituencies they represent in this House of Commons, they will never fail to represent their own people as they would be expected to.

speechtext: I think it is time I should intervene. All hon. members will admit that the Chair has been extremely lenient in the course of this debate. The rules have been violated on both sides of the house. A few days ago we had a general discussion on the first item of the estimates of the Department of National Defence. The discussion we are having now is a repetition of the general discussion we had the other day, and at times it has even a greater scope than the discussion that took place on the first item. Therefore I ask the co-operation of all members of the committee in confining their remarks to the item under discussion, item 250.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not quite able to apprehend the exact meaning of the remarks because I am not aware of what earlier speaker offended against the rules. I may have been out when it happened. During the remarks that I have been making I have been discussing the subject that has been before the house, and I had just asked a question of the Minister of National Defence when the hon. member for Temiscouata made certain statements which I think I should comment on briefly. I find myself in agreement with a great deal that the hon. member for Temiscouata has said. I most certainly am in complete agreement with him when he says that the question of national defence should be decided by the members of the House of Commons and the Senate. That has been my contention since these estimates were called on November 11.
The remarks I have been making have been directed to the hope that we might have the information which would make it possible for members of the house and members of the Senate to reach a decision with some knowledge of the facts. I do not want to have any exchange with regard to the individuals who have been mentioned which would in any way divert the discussion from what is before the house, but I would point out that no reasonable interpretation of any

remark I made could under any circumstances be suggested as a comparison, favourable or otherwise, between the hon. member for Nanaimo and any other hon. member in his capacity as a member of the House of Commons. What I pointed out was that in this particular field of responsibility the member who advocated such a drastic change in emphasis in the organization of our defence forces is a man with very wide experience. He started his service as a private, went through every N.C.O. and officer rank, and as a result of that very process as a regular soldier has a wealth of experience which he is able to pass on to us.
No remark that I made was a reflection in any way upon the service of the Minister of National Defence who served most gallantly in the artillery in the first world war. May I say that it is a matter that demonstrates the quality of his service that in that war he was awarded a decoration which I think most members will regard as second only to the V.C. in its recognition of valour. No remark of mine was intended as an unfavourable comparison, and I hope no hon. member will suggest that.
I think, however, that when we are discussing agriculture perhaps a skilled farmer knows a little more about agriculture than somebody else, although we must all exercise what judgment we can when we hear the farmers tell us what the facts are. I also think when it comes to the subject of health, although we must all pass judgment in regard to what is appropriate in the provision of health measures, it is proper that we should have some regard to the experience of those doctors whose qualifications enable them to express an expert opinion. We all must pass judgment. I would make this comment as to a remark made by the hon. member for Temiscouata which it seems to me is the strongest supporting argument I have heard yet in favour of the whole problem being discussed by a committee. He said: If you were dealing with a question of electricity and you were putting it before a judge you would not expect the judge to be an expert electrical engineer. No, we do not; but we do not expect the judge to pass judgment without hearing experts. We do not expect any judge to pass judgment unless he has had the opportunity of having evidence placed before him by those who are able to express an expert opinion in regard to that peculiarly technical subject.
At the present time we are dealing with one of the most complex problems that have ever confronted men and women who are

called upon to exercise their judgment, because today the defence forces of this or any other country combine the skill of electrical engineers, metallurgical engineers and engineers of every type, of industrial experts and producers as well as military men in their military formations. Today the defence forces are a combination of every productive and physical capacity of the country. It is for that very reason that, of all the subjects with which we are called upon to deal, no subject so clearly demands expert information before those of us who are not experts are in a position to pass judgment in the high court of parliament.
Let us take a few of the examples. During the last war science brought all its strength, all its skill and all its energy to the production of new devices, and it has not stood still. Today, if we assume our responsibility, we will make sure that within whatever defined field of responsibility we accept the task of preparing defence forces, they will be efficiently equipped in the most economical way, and with the very finest type of arms and equipment that can be supplied. When I say that I would emphasize the fact that in the last war Canada demonstrated that there is no intricate mechanism of war or of peace which the skilled workmen of this country, associated with our technicians and our management experts, are not capable of producing. For that reason we do need expert advice, and that is why I still press my suggestion that a committee would be the appropriate place.
I have interjected these remarks in relation to what has been just said. I would return now to the question I asked before those remarks were made: in the case of the army, what are the arms of that service today?

speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, this merely illustrates the evasion in answers that is presenting a very serious problem. This information is all committed to print. It is available to the armed services, as well as to others. I return to a comparison which will be in the minds of a number of people, no matter what decision may be reached on a motion that is to be presented tomorrow. It is no easier to determine whether a football team is ready for the test it has to meet than to determine whether or not we are really training and equipping our service units, unless we know what weapons they are supposed to have and what weapons they actually have at the present time.

speechtext:
If the hon. member has the information available to him I do not think he should delay the deliberations of this committee by asking for it, because certainly I do not have available, here and now, the establishment of arms, weapons and equipment or the training strengths of the armed forces of Canada. No one on earth could expect me to have that information, either, unless they were determined to hold up these estimates.
Now, sir, we have had some debate of a very general character over a period of three days, during which a number of hon. members have expressed various points of view. On November 18 the remarks of the leader of the opposition covered pages 1934 to 1943 of Hansard; he took over an hour of the time of this house to go through the white paper, without disagreeing with a single proposition in it. In his opening remarks this evening he said the minister had indicated his readiness to answer the questions that had been asked, and as far as I am aware up to this time no single question has been left unanswered. No single question has gone unanswered during the course of this whole debate, and I am prepared to answer all reasonable questions hon. members may put forward with respect to the defence forces of Canada. But if I am to be put through an interrogation respecting the arms manual and other things that are available to people at various levels, then I suggest we are wasting the time of this committee.
The leader of the opposition referred to the hon. member for Nanaimo. I can assure this committee that my respect, and I am sure the respect of all other hon. members, for the member for Nanaimo will not be reduced by anything the leader of the opposition said

Supply-National Defence this evening, because we hold the hon. gentleman in the highest regard. The hon. member for Nanaimo laid great emphasis on the air force, and I agree with him. That is the point; I agree with him. I just differ as to the practicability of providing an appropriation for the air force three times that of the army, at this time or in the immediate future.
In that connection I would point out, as I did before, that in the United States the proportion of expenditure as between the army, air force and navy, is 33'6 per cent for the army, 34 per cent for the air force and 32-4 per cent for the navy. In our estimates for this year, exclusive of defence research and provisions for pensions, our provisions on a comparable basis are for the army 36-4 per cent, for the air force 42-6 per cent and for the navy 21 per cent. In other words while in the United States they have made provision on an almost equal basis, in Canada we have recognized the position of the air force to the extent of giving it prior place by a very substantial margin. It is interesting to note that in the United Kingdom the defence pound is divided as between the army, air force and navy in the proportions of 43 per cent, 29 per cent and 28 per cent. There the air force is in the middle position. It is also interesting to note that in the second world war Canada's great contribution in men was roughly divided in this way: 600,000 to the army, 300,000 to the air force and 100,000 to the navy. So I submit that when the hon. member for Nanaimo, supported by the leader of the opposition, urges greater support for the air force, they are falling through an open door, because we are already doing what they ask and we are doing it to the full extent we believe possible within the limits of these estimates. In future appropriations I would hope, as I indicated when this matter came up on November 18, that this emphasis may be further increased.
This is indeed a complex problem, as the leader of the opposition has said. It has been found to be complex in every country, particularly at this time. We do not claim to know all the answers. We do not claim that anything we do may prove to be ultimately right, because we cannot look into the distant future. All we can try to do, with the help and support of this house and of the Canadian people, is to provide the funds which you and the people think desirable, and then allocate those funds among the three services as best we can. But I do submit that in our recognition of the very important place of the air force we have gone further than the other two countries with which we are so closely affiliated and associated in the most friendly fashion, and we are prepared to go even further.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all may I point out that since we are dealing with an item involving $339 million, I have no apologies for spending an hour in discussing what it implies, nor should any other member. I do not want to say that the Minister of National Defence obviously forgot what I said, or has not read what Hansard records, when he states that I agreed with what is set out in the white paper. I said the white paper gives us no real information as to the state of our defence forces. It gives us a broad picture in general terms, but we do not know the details.
I have asked a simple question dealing only with the first primary unit of our armed forces, an infantry battalion. My question was concerned with the weapon establishment of an infantry battalion on active service. If the hon. members of this house are to know with what we are dealing when they examine these figures, they should have an answer to that question as well as an answer to similar questions about the artillery, reconnaissance units, tank units, armoured units and each of the fifteen branches of the service incorporated in our land forces.
Then, we should know what percentage of weapons they have in relation to that establishment. Without that information we do not know what we are getting for our money, but above all we do not know what we are getting for the defence of Canada. It is a complete mystery, hidden by the answer that it is not in the public interest to give that information. Hon. members of this house have a right and a duty to know that, before they pass judgment. If this is not the place to get the information, then that is all the more reason why we should have a committee where, if it is desirable, any secret matter can be dealt with behind closed doors, following the minister's own suggestion that small committees are desirable in dealing with technical matters.
The minister has said he is not prepared to give that answer. He has not at his disposal the weapon establishment of all the units. I am satisfied that the weapon establishment is in the records that his officials have in front of him now. I would be surprised if they came here without that information. If we are to be confronted with this answer about the infantry, there is no use in pursuing the question further in regard to the other branches of the service. It is about time, however, that the members of this house recognized that they have a responsibility to know what we really have in the way of defence.
Here is a recruiting advertisement that appeared in the press of this country yesterday. It shows an anti-aircraft gun, and at the

top are the words, "Science turned their backs on the target." The meaning of those words is that science has made it possible for the men serving an anti-aircraft gun to fire at a target with their backs towards that target. This manoeuvre involves the intricate mechanisms which science has now made available for the control of anti-aircraft guns. No hon. member of this house is in a position to know how effective our expenditure on anti-aircraft guns is unless he knows how many anti-aircraft batteries there are in Canada, fully equipped with the latest short wave radar, equipped with electrical control devices, sound range devices, directional devices, and all the other intricate mechanisms by which these guns are fired. Nor are we in a position to know how effective those weapons are unless we know how many of the shells available for those weapons are fused with proximity fuses.
In order to ascertain the extent to which information is available, I am asking the Minister of National Defence how many shells there are in Canada fused with a proximity fuse?

speechtext: Not one.

I am not a member of the House of Commons of Great Britain, nor am I a member of the congress of the United States. So that there will be more laughter by those who wanted to find something to laugh about, I shall repeat that I am not a member of the House of Commons of Great Britain, nor of the congress of the United States. The members of those two illustrious bodies are in a position to secure the information which we are being denied.
The members of the congress of the United States, which the Minister of National Defence before he became minister thought afforded us an excellent example, are able to secure the most minute details of the organization of their forces, except in regard to those things that are still on the secret list. Proximity fuses are no longer on the secret list. In the closing days of the war proximity fuses were not only an essential requirement for effective anti-aircraft fire; they became an essential requirement of effective land artillery as well. Taken by itself, that indicates the extent to which we are absolutely unprepared in certain branches of the services to meet the tests of modern war.
Since we are not going to get the information about the weapon establishment of those units, I should like to refer to a speech made by the Minister of National Defence on May 2. An effort had been made earlier to obtain a statement about the decision as to the future equipment of our armed forces, but it was not forthcoming. I have heard no statement in the house during the consideration of these estimates which amplifies a statement that was made by the minister in Detroit on May 2. He said that Canada has decided to abandon the rim cartridge [DOT] 303 calibre rifle, machine guns of the same calibre, and to adopt weapons of United States standards as well as their communications organization and other details of organization. I am not questioning whether that is wise or unwise. Certainly since that statement was made in Detroit on May 2, I believe we should have

Supply-National Defence information as to the policy of the government in this respect, and when we propose to depart from our present weapon standards and adopt those of the United States.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
With regard to the last question, I think I pointed out on another occasion that the question of standardization was dealt with by me on two different occasions in this house, in which I indicated our desire to standardize our equipment with that of the United States and the United Kingdom. I thought that made sense. There has been no change in that policy, there has been no criticism of it and, so far as I know, it has been generally approved. It is, however, difficult of implementation. With regard to the rimless cartridge and the calibre, we have to wait on the determination, by those with whom we work, of their idea of the right kind of calibre. But we are prepared to co-operate with them just as, I am sure, are the armed forces of the United Kingdom and of the other ten countries in the North Atlantic security pact. We believe in standardization. As regards Canadian-United States co-operation, we believe that it is important to work to common industrial standards and common arms standards, and we are working in that direction. There has been no secret about that. It was announced during the war. It was worked on during the war and it has been continued ever since.
As the hon. leader of the opposition said, I referred to this matter in a speech on May 2; and I am sure that substantially he agrees with the general line.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think all hon. members will agree with the desirable features of standardization; but we still do not know just what the plans are other than that they will fit in with the modern adjustment of our forces. The Minister of National Defence is going to Paris to discuss the problem of the part that each of the member nations of the North Atlantic security pact will take in that combined effort. When we meet in the next session there will doubtless be a clearer understanding of the particular task which Canada has decided to undertake.
As to these present estimates, I have already pointed out that near the end of November we are not going to change greatly one way or another the expenditures that are made in 1949 or for the balance of the fiscal year because either the expenditures have been made or the commitments have already been made for the balance of the period. But what has been demonstrated here beyond any question is that when we deal with the estimates in the next session and are really examining them before they

are spent, we shall not have the necessary information unless we have a standing committee on the defence services of Canada.
I am not pressing the point further, because the minister has said that he will not answer the question in regard to the weapon establishment of our units. But I say that we definitely have a right to that information, and that when we know more of the general allocation of our forces, certainly the members of this committee should have full knowledge of the weapon establishment of each unit, how far we have gone or how far we expect to go in meeting those requirements of such units as we actually maintain.
As to these figures, we have indicated from the outset that we were not going to oppose them because the commitments have been made. But in voting for these estimates now, we do so recognizing that we have not the knowledge that we should have, that we have been denied information which every member needs if he is really going to pass judgment, and that when we meet in the next session we will insist then upon the establishment of a committee that will give us the information which will make it possible for us to fulfil our responsibilities as members of this parliament.

Thank you very much. I can give some details, certainly. The defence

research board is providing for central scientific and administrative organization-I can give it in round figures, in hundreds of thousands-$5,294,000; Canadian armament research and development establishment, $2,121,000; experimental station, Suffield, $2,301,000; defence research chemical laboratories, $459,000; Kingston laboratory $99,000; Grosse Isle experimental station, $50,000; radio propagation laboratories $686,000; naval research establishment, $563,000; defence research specific naval laboratory, $156,000; defence research northern laboratory, $315,000; a total of $12 million. Then for naval development, $447,000; for army development, $2,258,000; for air force development $6,952,000; a total of $21,179,000.
If I might say a word or two in general, defence research in Canada has been integrated with the work of the armed forces. The chairman of the defence research board is a member of the chiefs of staff committee; and the chiefs of staff are members of the defence research board; also on the defence research board are representatives of the national research council, the universities and industry. We believe there is a very complete integration of activities so as to eliminate duplication. We do not aim to cover the whole field of defence research in Canada. We could not do it with even $21 million. But in co-operation with the United States and the United Kingdom particularly, we are working on the things which are particularly suited to Canadian research either by reason of the personnel we have available or by reason of the industrial development of the country.
If I might refer to some of them briefly, I would mention the Canadian armament research and development establishment at Valcartier, which was especially developed during the war and further extended since, related particularly to the research in armaments, ballistics, propellants and the like, and their work is being carried on. The experimental station at Suffield, as hon. members know, is of course related to bacteriological and chemical warfare. At Suffield we have a great tract of almost a thousand square miles where we have opportunities and facilities for extensive trials.
Then, we are continuing to conduct research with regard to naval activities as they are particularly related to anti-submarine warfare, and we are extending our activities in the more applied field with regard to aircraft and aerodynamics. We provide a number of grants to Canadian universities to promote research. These are carefully worked out in conjunction with the national research council, and are designed to promote both fundamental and more applied research.

With regard to our development program, by far the largest item is that of nearly $7 million for air force development. During the war I think there were three translators who were used for the purpose I have mentioned. These three linguists were able to cover twenty-five languages. They were men who did translating for purposes of censorship during the war years. At the end of the war they were taken over by the Department of National Revenue to do this domestic reading. I have never been able to discover the truth of the matter either by questioning the

Minister of National Revenue or so far tonight. I have not been able to get specific information as to the point. I ask the Secretary of State whether since the war we have replaced these men, who were good linguists and top men in their profession, by anyone else who is capable of scrutinizing such material.
We have had a great deal of talk lately in this house and in the country generally about censorship. Much has been said about the admission to Canada of crime comics and books. I am not taking the position that I am advocating censorship. I do not want to be misunderstood about that, but I am interested in the general subject of books. We can do with a lot more books in this country. If we are going to have censorship, if we are going to exclude from Canada foreign language books which are excluded simply through the ignorance of the people who are handling the matter, then I am opposed to that method of doing business. You will excuse me if I am a little heated about this particular subject, but I have been fighting against a stone wall for two or three years, and this is one of those hidden recesses of government which I have not been able to penetrate up to the present time. That is the reason why I thought I would bring the matter up tonight. I notice that the Minister of National Revenue is flattering me by rather earnest attention, and I hope when his turn comes he will be able to give me an answer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I can give you the answer now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I realize that the Secretary of State is new to his position. I do not think anyone will hold it against him if he is not schooled in this particular matter, but it is a subject into which I have been making investigations. So far as I am concerned, I believe that the examination of foreign language books has been quite haphazard. I think a great many of them are worthy of being admitted. A great many of them which are worthy of being admitted are kept out simply because there are not people learned enough in these languages to examine them properly. I also believe the converse is true. We are admitting a lot of stuff we should not be admitting for the same reason. I know for a fact that books which are being denied entry at one customs port are being admitted at others. The whole situation is confused. If you do not believe it, look at the bookstands. I have known of cases when customs officers were simply flabbergasted. An officer is confronted with a foreign book about which he knows nothing.

He may take it to a Greek restaurateur and ask, "Is this book all right?" The Greek gentleman says it is all right, and that is the basis on which censorship is carried out in this country, the basis on which books are either accepted or rejected. It is time that situation was brought to an end. It is time the importation of suitable books into this country was encouraged. It is time we had men at the head of this censorship branch who are qualified by their background, their training, their education and by some elementary knowledge of literature to say what is good and what is bad; and I am not speaking in the moral sense, but rather in the literary sense. If the Secretary of State has no further information for me, however, I suppose we will have to leave it at that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The only information I can give the hon. member is that we do what translations are done. If any department of the government needs someone to read something in a foreign language, we do not know anything about that. We do the translation and provide them with it. That goes from our department; but I know nothing about anything else.
